lessons.title: Sit, hold, and your first stroke
lessons.summary: How to set up at the kit, hold the sticks so they rebound, and play one even stroke.
objectives: You will set a stool and snare to your own height
You will hold a stick so it bounces instead of being forced
You will play 20 even single strokes
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Set the stool so your thighs slope slightly down and your heel can lift
- Find the balance point of the stick, about a third from the butt
- Play singles on the snare: R L R L, slow and even

## Understand it

Good drumming starts before the first stroke — with how you sit and hold the sticks. Bad habits here cause tension, slow hands and, over years, pain in the wrists and back.

**Setting up:**

- **Stool height** — thighs slope slightly **down** from hip to knee, so the feet can work the pedals and the heel can lift. Too low and your legs tire; too high and you lose balance.
- **Distance** — you can reach every drum and cymbal without leaning or stretching.
- **Posture** — back straight but relaxed, shoulders down, arms hanging naturally.

**The grip (matched grip):** both hands hold the sticks the same way.

- Find the **fulcrum** — the balance point, roughly a third of the way up from the butt end. Pinch the stick there between the thumb and the first joint of the index (or middle) finger.
- The other fingers wrap **loosely** around the stick — supporting it, not squeezing.
- **German grip** has palms facing down (more power); **French grip** has thumbs on top (more finger control); **American grip** sits between them. Most drummers start with American.

**The first stroke — let the stick bounce:**

- Lift the stick with the wrist, drop it into the drum, and **let it rebound** back up. Do not press it into the head; that chokes the sound and tires your hand.
- Think of **dribbling a ball** — the drum does half the work.

Play strokes slowly, alternating hands (R L R L), and listen for **even volume** between hands.

## Key words

- **Fulcrum:** the pinch point where the stick balances in the hand
- **Matched grip:** both hands holding the sticks the same way
- **Rebound:** the stick bouncing back off the drum head
- **Stroke:** one hit of the stick on the drum

## Read and watch

- [Drum: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/drums/) — Yamaha
- [Drumming education](https://vicfirth.zildjian.com/education) — Vic Firth

## Practise at home

1. Eight minutes of singles on a pillow or your knees, counting out loud
1. Ten slow strokes with each hand alone, watching the stick rebound

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Play it at half speed with the metronome until it is clean, then add 10 bpm. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play it with your weak hand leading, add ghost notes, and teach the groove to someone in the class.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Play 60 seconds of single strokes at a steady slow tempo without the sticks sticking in the head.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Pulse: counting, and the metronome
lessons.summary: The pulse underneath everything, counted out loud and played with a click.
objectives: You will count 1-2-3-4 out loud while playing
You will play quarter notes with a metronome at 60 bpm
You will say what a bar is
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Clap the pulse of three songs the class chooses
- Play quarter notes on the snare with the metronome at 60, then 70
- Count out loud the whole time — if you stop counting, stop playing

## Understand it

The **pulse** (or beat) is the steady heartbeat under music — what you tap your foot to. A drummer's first job in any band is to **keep the pulse steady**, so everyone else can rely on it.

**Tempo** is how fast the pulse goes, measured in **beats per minute (bpm)**. 60 bpm is one beat every second; 120 bpm is two per second. Afrobeats songs often sit around 100–115 bpm; slow ballads 60–80; fast fuji or highlife can go much higher.

**Counting:** most popular music is in **4/4 time** — four beats in each bar. Count "**1, 2, 3, 4**" over and over. Beat 1 is the strongest — the start of the bar.

**The metronome** clicks a perfectly steady pulse. Practising with it shows you where you **rush** (speed up — very common when excited or playing loud) or **drag** (slow down — common on hard passages). Free metronome apps are fine.

How to practise with it:

1. Start **slow** — slower than you think you need (60 bpm).
2. Play quarter notes (one per beat), and try to make your stroke land exactly on the click so the click "disappears".
3. Only speed up by small steps (4–5 bpm) when it is perfect.

Playing slowly in time is harder than playing fast — and far more valuable.

## Key words

- **Pulse:** the steady beat underneath music
- **Tempo:** the speed of the pulse, in beats per minute
- **Bar (measure):** a group of beats, usually four
- **Metronome:** a device that clicks a steady tempo

## Read and watch

- [Make beats](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-beats/make-beats.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Five minutes a day with a free metronome app at 60 bpm
1. Count along to one song you love and find beat 1

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Play it at half speed with the metronome until it is clean, then add 10 bpm. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play it with your weak hand leading, add ghost notes, and teach the groove to someone in the class.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Play 16 bars of quarter notes at 70 bpm with the click, counting aloud.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: The backbeat
lessons.summary: Kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4 — the groove under most popular music.
objectives: You will play kick on 1 and 3 and snare on 2 and 4
You will keep it steady for a minute
You will name the backbeat in a song you hear
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Kick alone on 1 and 3, then snare alone on 2 and 4
- Put them together slowly, 60 bpm
- Listen to a song and clap only on 2 and 4

## Understand it

The **backbeat** is the foundation of most popular music — rock, pop, R&B, gospel, hip-hop, much of Afrobeats. It is simple:

- **Bass drum (kick)** on beats **1 and 3**.
- **Snare** on beats **2 and 4** — the "backbeat", the beats you clap on.

The snare on 2 and 4 is what makes music feel like it moves forward and makes people want to dance. Clap along to almost any pop song and you will clap on 2 and 4.

**Learning it:**

1. Kick alone on 1 and 3 — foot steady, pedal returning each time.
2. Snare alone on 2 and 4.
3. Together, **slowly** (60 bpm). Count aloud: "**1** (kick) **2** (snare) **3** (kick) **4** (snare)".

**Coordination** — getting hands and feet to do different things — is the drummer's special skill, and the brain builds it through slow, correct repetition. If it falls apart, slow down; do not push through mistakes, or you practise the mistake.

**Listen** to how songs vary the backbeat: kicks added between (on "and"s), the snare replaced by claps or rimshots, or (in many Afrobeats grooves) the pattern shifted so the "backbeat" is felt differently. The basic backbeat is the reference all of those vary.

## Key words

- **Backbeat:** snare on beats 2 and 4
- **Kick (bass drum):** the big low drum played with the foot pedal
- **Coordination:** limbs playing different parts at once
- **Groove:** a repeating rhythm pattern that feels good to move to

## Read and watch

- [Make beats](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-beats/make-beats.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Drum: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/drums/) — Yamaha

## Practise at home

1. Three minutes of kick and snare only, no hi-hat, at 60 bpm
1. Find the backbeat in two songs and tap it on your leg

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Play it at half speed with the metronome until it is clean, then add 10 bpm. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play it with your weak hand leading, add ghost notes, and teach the groove to someone in the class.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Play the kick-and-snare backbeat for one minute at 70 bpm, clean and even.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Eighth notes on the hi-hat
lessons.summary: Adding the hi-hat over the backbeat, and keeping three limbs independent.
objectives: You will play eight hi-hat notes to a bar
You will add the kick and snare under them
You will count 1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Hi-hat alone, eight to a bar, counting "1 and 2 and"
- Add snare on 2 and 4
- Add kick on 1 and 3 — slowly, it will fall apart at first

## Understand it

Adding **eighth notes** on the hi-hat turns a basic backbeat into a full **rock/pop groove**, the beat behind thousands of songs.

**Eighth notes** split each beat in two, so there are **eight in a bar of 4/4**. Count them: "**1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and**". The numbers are the beats; the "ands" fall exactly halfway between.

**Building the groove in layers:**

1. **Hi-hat alone** — eight even strokes per bar, counting aloud. Keep the hi-hat closed (foot pressing the pedal down) for a tight "tss".
2. **Add snare** on 2 and 4 — the hand on the hi-hat keeps going; the other hand hits the snare. (Right-handed drummers usually cross: right hand on hi-hat, left on snare.)
3. **Add kick** on 1 and 3.

When the three lock together, every snare and kick hit lands **exactly with** a hi-hat stroke.

**Even eighths:** the hi-hat strokes should be the same volume and the same distance apart. Record yourself — uneven hi-hats are the most common sign of a beginner.

**Accent the beat:** many drummers play the hi-hat slightly louder on the numbers and softer on the "ands" — this adds a natural swing and pulse.

Practise at 60 bpm, then slowly speed up. Most pop songs use this groove at 90–130 bpm.

## Key words

- **Eighth note:** half a beat — eight in a bar of 4/4
- **Hi-hat:** two cymbals on a stand, opened and closed by a foot pedal
- **Subdivision:** dividing beats into smaller equal parts
- **Accent:** a note played louder than those around it

## Read and watch

- [Make beats](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/make-beats/make-beats.html) — Ableton Learning Music
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

## Practise at home

1. Four minutes at 55 bpm. If it breaks down, go slower, not faster
1. Hi-hat and kick only, then hi-hat and snare only, then all three

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Play it at half speed with the metronome until it is clean, then add 10 bpm. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play it with your weak hand leading, add ghost notes, and teach the groove to someone in the class.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Play the full beat — hi-hat eighths, snare on 2 and 4, kick on 1 and 3 — for 16 bars.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Fills
lessons.summary: Moving round the kit and landing back on beat 1.
objectives: You will play a one-bar fill in eighth notes
You will land on beat 1 of the next bar
You will count through the fill
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play three bars of groove, one bar of fill, repeat
- Fill: four strokes on snare, four on the tom, then crash on 1
- The crash on beat 1 is the point — the fill is only the run-up

## Understand it

A **fill** is a short break from the groove — usually at the end of a section — that signals "something is changing": the chorus is coming, the verse is ending, the song is about to stop. Fills give songs shape and tell the band and audience where they are.

**The golden rule: the groove must come back exactly on time.** A flashy fill that lands late on beat 1 is worse than no fill at all. Beat 1 after the fill — usually marked with a **crash cymbal and kick together** — is the most important note.

**Your first fill:**

- Play **three bars of groove**, then **one bar of fill**, and repeat. This is the "four-bar phrase" songs are built from.
- Fill: four strokes on the snare, then four on the toms (high tom to floor tom) — eighth notes, counting "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and".
- Land the crash and kick on beat 1 of the next bar, and go straight back into the groove.

**Making fills musical:**

- **Start simple** — one beat of fill is often enough.
- **Leave space** — a fill does not need to be full of notes.
- **Move around the kit** in one direction, like a phrase going downwards.
- Count every fill aloud while you learn it.

The **rudiments** (basic sticking patterns like single strokes RLRL, double strokes RRLL, paradiddles RLRR LRLL) are the vocabulary fills are made from.

## Key words

- **Fill:** a short break from the groove, leading into a new section
- **Phrase:** a musical sentence, often four bars long
- **Crash:** a loud cymbal used to mark the start of a section
- **Rudiment:** a basic sticking pattern drummers practise

## Read and watch

- [International drum rudiments](https://pas.org/rudiments/) — Percussive Arts Society
- [Drumming education](https://vicfirth.zildjian.com/education) — Vic Firth

## Practise at home

1. Three bars of groove plus one bar of fill, eight times, at 60 bpm
1. Try the same fill starting on the tom instead

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Play it at half speed with the metronome until it is clean, then add 10 bpm. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play it with your weak hand leading, add ghost notes, and teach the groove to someone in the class.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Play eight bars: groove for three, fill for one, twice, landing on the crash each time.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Afrobeat: the feel Tony Allen built
lessons.summary: The looser, busier hi-hat and ghost notes that make an Afrobeat groove move.
objectives: You will play ghost notes on the snare
You will play a 16th-note hi-hat pattern
You will say how Afrobeat differs from a straight rock beat
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Listen to Tony Allen with Fela — count the bar and find the snare
- Play soft ghost notes between the backbeats
- Open the hi-hat on the last eighth of the bar

## Understand it

**Afrobeat** — the music **Fela Anikulapo Kuti** created in Lagos in the late 1960s and 1970s — is built on the drumming of **Tony Allen** (1940–2020). Fela himself said that without Tony Allen there would be no Afrobeat. Tony Allen combined jazz drumming, highlife, funk and Yoruba rhythms into a style that drummers around the world still study.

What makes his feel different from a rock backbeat:

- **Independence** — all four limbs play their own interlocking patterns, rather than hands and feet doubling one another.
- **Ghost notes** — very quiet snare strokes between the main hits, felt more than heard. They fill the space and give the groove its rolling, conversational texture.
- **The kick moves** — it does not sit on 1 and 3; it dances around the bar, interacting with the bass.
- **Open and closed hi-hat** patterns give lift and accent.
- **Restraint** — the groove stays relaxed and steady for many minutes, with variation in small details.

Practising ghost notes: play your snare backbeat at normal volume, then add strokes between at **very low height** — the stick only a few centimetres above the head. The contrast between loud accents and quiet ghosts is the skill.

(Afrobeat is different from **Afrobeats** — the modern pop genre of Burna Boy, Wizkid and Davido — though Afrobeats draws on it.)

## Key words

- **Afrobeat:** the genre Fela Kuti and Tony Allen created in 1970s Lagos
- **Ghost note:** a very quiet note felt more than heard
- **Independence:** each limb playing its own pattern
- **Afrobeats:** the modern West African pop genre

## Read and watch

- [Search: Tony Allen](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=tony%20allen) — Google Arts & Culture
- [Search: Fela Kuti](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=fela%20kuti) — Google Arts & Culture

## Practise at home

1. Five minutes of ghost notes at low volume — they must be quiet to work
1. Play along with one Afrobeat track, just hi-hat and kick

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Play it at half speed with the metronome until it is clean, then add 10 bpm. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play it with your weak hand leading, add ghost notes, and teach the groove to someone in the class.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Play eight bars of an Afrobeat groove with ghost notes you can hear are quieter than the backbeat.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Looking back: three grooves from memory
lessons.summary: Returning to the grooves of weeks 3 to 6 without the music in front of you, which is the test of whether they are learnt.
objectives: You will play three earlier grooves from memory
You will move between them without stopping
You will say which one is weakest and why
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play the week 3 backbeat, the week 4 eighth-note groove and the week 6 Afrobeat, four bars each
- Change between them on the bar line, no gaps
- Record it on a phone and listen back

## Understand it

Six weeks in, you have three grooves: the **backbeat** (week 3), the **eighth-note groove** (week 4) and an **Afrobeat** pattern (week 6). Playing them from memory, back to back, tests two things that matter in a band: whether you really know them, and whether you can **switch between them without losing time**.

**The exercise:** four bars of each, in order, with no stop between them, at a steady tempo with the metronome. Then try it with a fill at the end of each four-bar section.

**What to check — record it and listen back:**

- **Tempo** — does it rush when you change groove? Most drummers speed up at transitions.
- **Evenness** — are the hi-hats regular? Are the snare hits the same volume?
- **Feel** — does the Afrobeat sound relaxed, with clear ghost notes, or stiff?
- **Transitions** — does beat 1 of each new groove land exactly in time?

**Memory and practice:** music you can only play while reading or thinking hard is not yet learnt. The goal is **automaticity** — the groove plays itself, leaving your attention free to listen to the band. That comes from many short, correct repetitions spread over days, far better than one long session the night before.

Write down which groove is weakest, and give it the most practice this week.

## Key words

- **Transition:** moving from one section or groove to another
- **Automaticity:** playing without having to think about each movement
- **Rushing:** unintentionally speeding up

## Read and watch

- [Drumming education](https://vicfirth.zildjian.com/education) — Vic Firth
- [International drum rudiments](https://pas.org/rudiments/) — Percussive Arts Society

## Practise at home

1. Run the three grooves again every day this week, four bars each
1. Spend the extra time on the weakest one, slowly

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Play it at half speed with the metronome until it is clean, then add 10 bpm. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.
- **If you already can:** Play it with your weak hand leading, add ghost notes, and teach the groove to someone in the class.

## Assessed this week

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: The dùndún: the drum that talks
lessons.summary: The Yoruba talking drum, how its tension changes pitch, and why it follows speech.
objectives: You will change the pitch of a dùndún with arm pressure
You will play a simple speech phrase on it
You will say why Yoruba tone makes this possible
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Hold the drum under the arm and squeeze to raise the pitch
- Play a three-syllable phrase in low-mid-high tones
- Listen to a master drummer and follow the rise and fall

## Understand it

The Yoruba **dùndún** is the famous "talking drum": an hourglass-shaped drum with two heads joined by leather cords running down its sides. Held under the arm and struck with a curved stick, its **pitch changes** as the player squeezes the cords — tighter cords stretch the heads and the note rises; relaxing them lowers it.

**Why it can talk:** Yoruba is a **tonal language** — the same syllables mean different things depending on whether they are said with a high, mid or low pitch. The dùndún copies these pitch patterns (and the rhythm of speech), so skilled drummers can play phrases, proverbs, praise names (*oríkì*) and messages that Yoruba listeners understand.

**The dùndún ensemble** includes:

- **Ìyá ìlù** ("mother drum") — the lead, which "talks".
- **Omele** — smaller supporting drums playing repeating patterns.
- **Gúdúgúdú** — a small kettle-shaped drum.

Talking drums are central to Yoruba ceremonies, praise singing, and to music such as **jùjú** (King Sunny Adé made the talking drum famous worldwide) and **fújì**.

**Playing it:** the drum hangs from the shoulder under the arm (left arm for most); the arm squeezes the cords; the stick strikes the head. Practise a sliding pitch — strike, then squeeze — and a three-syllable phrase following the tones of a word you know.

Respect its role: the talking drum carries words and praise, and some phrases are for particular people and occasions.

## Key words

- **Dùndún:** the Yoruba hourglass talking drum
- **Tonal language:** a language where pitch changes word meaning
- **Ìyá ìlù:** the lead 'mother' drum of the ensemble
- **Oríkì:** Yoruba praise poetry, often drummed

## Read and watch

- [Search: talking drum](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=talking%20drum) — Google Arts & Culture
- [Art of Africa](https://www.khanacademy.org/humanities/art-africa) — Khan Academy

## Practise at home

1. Practise squeezing and releasing while striking — pitch, not rhythm, is the exercise
1. Say your own name in tones, then play it

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Play it at half speed with the metronome until it is clean, then add 10 bpm. Two clean minutes beat twenty messy ones.

lessons.title: Dynamics: loud, soft, and accents
lessons.summary: Playing the same pattern at three volumes, and placing an accent where you choose.
objectives: You will play a groove quietly and loudly on purpose
You will accent a chosen note in a pattern
You will say why a quiet drummer is more useful than a loud one
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play the week 4 groove as quietly as you can, then as loudly as is still controlled
- Play eight hi-hat notes with an accent on 1 and 3 only
- Play behind someone singing — you must be quieter than them

## Understand it

**Dynamics** — how loud or soft music is — are what make drumming musical rather than mechanical. Drummers are often told to play softer, rarely louder; control at low volume is the mark of a good drummer.

The Italian terms musicians use:

- **pp** (*pianissimo*) — very soft
- **p** (*piano*) — soft
- **mp / mf** — moderately soft / moderately loud
- **f** (*forte*) — loud
- **ff** (*fortissimo*) — very loud
- **Crescendo** — getting gradually louder; **diminuendo** — getting gradually softer.

**On drums, volume comes from stick height**, not from force:

- Low stick (a few cm) — soft.
- High stick (from the wrist, 20+ cm) — loud.
- Same relaxed stroke and rebound every time; only the height changes.
- Hitting harder with a low stick makes a choked, ugly sound and tires you.

**Accents:** a louder note in a line of softer ones. Exercise: eight eighth notes on the snare, accenting one at a time (first, then second, then third…). Use **height**: accent strokes start high and stay high; soft strokes stay low. Drummers call these **full strokes** and **taps**.

Play your week 4 groove as quietly as possible while still clear and steady, then as loud as you can while still in control. Most beginners find the quiet version harder — and most gigs need it.

## Key words

- **Dynamics:** the loudness or softness of music
- **Crescendo:** getting gradually louder
- **Accent:** a note played louder than those around it
- **Stick height:** how high the stick starts — it controls volume

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

1. Accent practice: eight strokes, accent moving one position each time

lessons.title: Playing with other people
lessons.summary: Locking with a bass player, listening more than you play, and following a song.
objectives: You will lock the kick with a bass line
You will follow a song through its sections
You will stop when the band stops
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play with a bass player or a recorded bass line — match the kick to the bass notes
- Follow a song: intro, verse, chorus, and mark each change with a fill
- Practise stopping dead on a cue

## Understand it

Playing alone, you only have to keep time with yourself. In a band, the drummer **leads** the time for everyone — and that means listening more than playing.

**Lock with the bass.** The drummer and bass player together are the **rhythm section**. The tightest bands have the **kick drum playing with the bass notes** — they land together, making one strong, low sound. Listen to the bass line and match your kick pattern to it.

**Follow the song's structure.** Know where you are — verse, chorus, bridge — and how many bars each lasts. A fill at the end of each section helps the band follow too.

**Cues.** Bands communicate with eye contact, nods and pre-agreed signals: the leader's raised hand for the ending, a nod for the chorus. Watch the leader; they may change the plan live (repeat a chorus, extend a solo). In church bands and live shows this is constant.

**Count in.** The drummer usually starts the song: four clicks on the sticks ("1, 2, 3, 4") at the **exact** tempo. Count in too fast and the whole song is too fast. Think of the song's tempo before you count.

**Serve the song.** Play what the music needs, not everything you can play. Space lets the singer and other instruments be heard.

**Endings** — practise them: a hit together on beat 1, or a crash and let ring. Clean endings make a band sound professional.

## Key words

- **Rhythm section:** drums and bass (often with keys or guitar) that hold the groove
- **Count-in:** clicks that set the tempo before the band starts
- **Cue:** a signal for the band to change or stop
- **Song form:** the order of sections: verse, chorus, bridge

## Read and watch

- [Play with song structures](https://learningmusic.ableton.com/song-structure/song-structure.html) — Ableton Learning Music

1. Count the bars of a verse so you know when the chorus arrives

lessons.title: Reading a drum chart
lessons.summary: What the lines and spaces mean on a drum stave, and how to follow a chart through a song.
objectives: You will name the positions for kick, snare and hi-hat
You will read and play a four-bar chart
You will follow repeat marks
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn the stave positions: kick bottom space, snare third space, hi-hat above the top line with an x
- Read a four-bar groove and play it
- Follow a chart with repeats and a coda

## Understand it

Drum music is written on a five-line **stave** (staff), but instead of pitches each line and space stands for a **drum or cymbal**. Reading it lets you learn songs faster, play from charts in bands and churches, and write your own grooves down.

**The usual positions** (they vary slightly between publishers; most charts include a key):

- **Bass drum (kick)** — bottom space.
- **Snare** — third space from the bottom.
- **Toms** — top spaces (high tom) down to the floor tom in the second space.
- **Hi-hat** — above the top line, written with an **x** notehead.
- **Ride and crash cymbals** — on or above the top line, with x noteheads.
- **Hi-hat with the foot** — below the stave, x notehead.

The stave begins with a **percussion clef** (two vertical lines) and a time signature (4/4).

**Rhythm values** are the same as in all music: **quarter note** (1 beat, filled head with stem), **eighth note** (½ beat, with a flag or beamed in pairs), **sixteenth** (¼ beat, two flags or beams), with **rests** for silences.

**Charts** often use shorthand: **repeat signs**, "**%**" (repeat the last bar), "fill" written over a bar, section markings (A, B, Chorus), **first and second endings**.

Practise by reading one bar at a time slowly, counting aloud.

## Key words

- **Stave (staff):** five lines on which music is written
- **Percussion clef:** two vertical lines showing unpitched drum notation
- **Notehead:** the round or x-shaped part of a written note
- **Chart:** a simplified written guide to a song

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

1. Read and clap one new four-bar chart a day
1. Write out the week 4 groove yourself, then play what you wrote
1. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain one drum notation symbol you are unsure of, then check what it says against the chart in front of you — if the symbol does not appear on your chart the way it described, it was wrong.

lessons.title: Term showcase
lessons.summary: Playing a prepared piece in front of the class, with the grooves and fills of the term in it.
objectives: You will perform a prepared piece from memory
You will play with at least one other musician
You will take and use one note from the audience
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Perform your piece — groove, one fill, a dynamic change, and a clean ending
- Play with a second musician or a backing track
- Listen to two classmates and give each one useful note

## Understand it

Your showcase piece should show everything you have learnt in a short, finished performance: a **groove**, at least **one fill**, a **dynamic change**, and a **clean ending**.

**Preparing:**

- Plan the structure on paper — e.g. 4-bar count-in, 8 bars groove, fill, 8 bars louder groove, fill, 4 bars soft, ending.
- Practise with the metronome until secure, then **without** it, keeping it steady.
- Run it **from start to finish** many times, including when you make mistakes — performers keep going.
- Practise the start and the ending most — the audience remembers them.

**On the day:**

- **Check the kit** — stool height, distances, pedal tension; adjust it to *you* (the last drummer had different legs).
- Warm up: slow singles and doubles on a practice pad or your leg.
- **Breathe**, think of the tempo (sing a bar of the groove in your head), then count in.

**During:** if you make a mistake, **do not stop and do not show it** — keep the time going and rejoin. The audience notices a stop; they rarely notice a missed note.

**After:** listen to a recording. Name **one thing that went well** and **one thing to practise next term**.

Playing with a second player (bass, keyboard, or the class) is a bonus — locking with someone else is what drummers are for.

## Key words

- **Structure:** the planned order of sections in a piece
- **Run-through:** performing from start to end without stopping
- **Recovery:** carrying on smoothly after a mistake

- [Drumming education](https://vicfirth.zildjian.com/education) — Vic Firth

lessons.title: Holding the violin and the bow
lessons.summary: Getting the instrument onto the shoulder without gripping, and holding a bow that can still move.
objectives: You will hold the violin without squeezing with your chin
You will form a bow hold with a bent thumb
You will name the four open strings
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Set the shoulder rest; the violin should balance without your left hand
- Bow hold: bent thumb against the frog, fingers curved, little finger on top
- Name and pluck the open strings: G D A E

## Understand it

The violin is one of the hardest instruments to start, because **both hands do completely different, delicate jobs** — and the way you hold it affects every note you will ever play. Time spent here saves years of fixing habits later.

**The parts:** the **body** (hollow wooden box), **neck** and **fingerboard** (no frets — you find each note by ear), four **strings** tuned **G D A E** from lowest to highest, the **bridge** holding the strings up, **pegs** and **fine tuners**, the **chinrest**, and the **shoulder rest**.

**Holding the violin:**

- It rests on the **left collarbone**, held by the **weight of the head** on the chinrest — not by clamping or lifting the shoulder.
- The **shoulder rest** fills the gap so it balances without the left hand.
- The scroll points **forward and slightly left**, roughly level.
- The left hand supports the neck loosely; the wrist is straight, not collapsed under the neck.

**The bow hold** — the hardest part:

- The **thumb is bent**, its tip touching the stick near the frog.
- The **fingers drape** over the stick, relaxed and curved; the **little finger is curved on top** of the stick, balancing it.
- No squeezing: a tense bow hold makes a scratchy, shaking sound.

Check in a mirror often. **Bow hair** must be tightened (only until there is a pencil's width between hair and stick) and **rosined** before playing, and loosened afterwards.

## Key words

- **Bow hold:** the curved-thumb, relaxed-finger grip of the bow
- **Rosin:** resin rubbed on bow hair to make it grip the string
- **Bridge:** the wooden piece holding the strings above the body
- **Open string:** a string played without a finger on it

## Read and watch

- [Violin: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/violin/) — Yamaha
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Two minutes a day of putting the violin up and taking it down
1. Make the bow hold, let go, and make it again — twenty times

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Practise the bow arm on open strings before adding fingers. Tone first, notes second.
- **If you already can:** Play it from memory at a faster tempo, then play the same tune starting on a different string.

lessons.title: Drawing a straight bow
lessons.summary: Long bows on open strings, parallel to the bridge, which is where tone comes from.
objectives: You will draw a full bow on one string without hitting another
You will keep the bow parallel to the bridge
You will say what makes a scratchy sound
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Long slow bows on open D, watching the bow stay parallel to the bridge
- Play at the halfway point between bridge and fingerboard
- Try bowing too close to the bridge and hear what happens

## Understand it

Violin tone comes from the **bow**. A beautiful sound depends on three things the right arm controls — the **contact point**, the **bow speed** and the **weight** (pressure) — and on keeping the bow **straight**.

**Straight bow:** the bow must move **parallel to the bridge**, all the way from the frog to the tip. If it slides at an angle, it drifts towards the fingerboard (thin, airy sound) or the bridge (glassy, squeaky sound).

Why it is hard: the arm moves in arcs, but the bow must go in a straight line. So the **elbow opens and the arm moves forward** as you approach the tip, and comes back as you return to the frog.

**The contact point:** usually about halfway between the bridge and the end of the fingerboard.

**Bow speed and weight work together:**

- More weight + slower bow → strong, rich tone.
- Less weight + faster bow → lighter, airier tone.
- Too much weight for the speed → crunching.
- Too little → whistling, thin sound.

**Down-bow** (moving from frog to tip) and **up-bow** (tip to frog) are marked on music with ⊓ and V.

**Practise in front of a mirror**: long, slow bows on the **open D string**, watching the bow stay parallel to the bridge. Then try the halfway point of the bow, then the tip area. Listen for an **even** sound from start to end of each stroke.

## Key words

- **Contact point:** where the bow touches the string
- **Down-bow:** bowing from the frog to the tip
- **Up-bow:** bowing from the tip to the frog
- **Tone:** the quality of the sound

lessons.summary: Where fingers 1, 2 and 3 fall on the A and E strings, and your first scale.
objectives: You will place fingers 1, 2 and 3 in first position

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Tape or mark the first position if your instructor does that
- Play A B C# D on the A string, then E F# G# A on the E string
- Check the note A on the E string against the open A

## Understand it

On the violin there are no frets — every note's **intonation** (exact pitch) depends on where the finger lands. Starting with a scale teaches the hand the **shape** it needs.

**First position, A string:**

- **Open A** (no finger)
- **1st finger → B**
- **2nd finger → C♯** (placed close to the 3rd finger)
- **3rd finger → D**

Then continue on the **E string**: **open E**, 1 → **F♯**, 2 → **G♯**, 3 → **A**. Those eight notes are the **A major scale**: A B C♯ D E F♯ G♯ A.

**Why fingers are placed at different distances:** a major scale has a pattern of **tones (whole steps) and semitones (half steps)** — T T S T T T S. On the fingerboard, a **semitone is a small gap** (fingers touching) and a **tone is a larger gap**. In A major, fingers 2 and 3 are close together — the "**2–3 pattern**" or "high 2".

**Finding the notes:**

- Many teachers use **tape markers** at first — helpful, but listen, do not just look.
- Check with a **tuner** app, or against an open string: the 3rd finger D on the A string should **ring** in sympathy with the open D string when it is in tune.

**Fingers:** curved, landing on the fingertips, close to the string — not lifted high above it. Keep fingers down where possible as you go up the scale.

## Key words

- **Intonation:** playing exactly in tune
- **First position:** the left hand nearest the scroll
- **Tone and semitone:** a whole step and a half step
- **Finger pattern:** the spacing of fingers for a key

## Read and watch

- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

lessons.summary: The treble stave, the notes you can already play, and matching paper to fingers.
objectives: You will name the notes on the treble stave
You will find a written note on the fingerboard
You will play a four-bar written line
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn the lines and spaces: E G B D F, F A C E
- Match five written notes to fingers on the A string
- Play a four-bar written melody slowly

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain a notation symbol you do not recognise, then find that symbol in the music in front of you. If it does not appear there the way it described, it was wrong.

## Understand it

Violin music is written in the **treble clef** (G clef), whose curl wraps around the **second line from the bottom — G above middle C**.

The five **lines** of the stave, from bottom to top, are **E G B D F** ("Every Good Boy Deserves Fruit"); the four **spaces** spell **F A C E**. Notes above or below the stave use short extra lines called **ledger lines**.

**Where the strings are written:**

- **Open G** — below the stave (three ledger lines down).
- **Open D** — just below the bottom line (the space below the stave).
- **Open A** — the second space.
- **Open E** — the top space.

**Matching notes to fingers on the A string:** A (2nd space, open), B (middle line, 1st finger), C♯ (3rd space, 2nd finger), D (4th line, 3rd finger).

**Key signatures:** sharps or flats written at the start of every line apply to all those notes. **A major** has **three sharps (F♯, C♯, G♯)**; **D major** has **two (F♯, C♯)**. If you see the sharps at the start, you do not need them written again by each note.

**Learning to read:**

- Say the note names aloud, then the finger numbers, then play.
- Read a little **every day** — reading improves with frequency more than with long sessions.
- Use flashcard tools (see the links) to build speed.

## Key words

- **Treble clef:** the G clef, curling around the G line
- **Ledger line:** a short extra line above or below the stave
- **Key signature:** sharps or flats at the start of each line
- **Sharp (♯):** raises a note by a semitone

lessons.title: Rhythm: quarters, eighths and rests
lessons.summary: Counting while you bow, and giving a rest its full length.
objectives: You will play quarter and eighth notes in time
You will count a bar out loud while playing
You will hold a rest for its full value
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Clap the rhythm before you play it, every time
- Play a line mixing quarters and eighths at 60 bpm
- Play a line with rests — stop the bow, do not rush

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys A B C#5 D5 E5 F#5 G#5
```

## Understand it

Rhythm tells you **how long** each note lasts, against the steady beat.

The basic values in 4/4 time:

- **Semibreve (whole note)** — 4 beats, an open note head with no stem.
- **Minim (half note)** — 2 beats, open head with stem.
- **Crotchet (quarter note)** — 1 beat, filled head with stem.
- **Quaver (eighth note)** — ½ beat, with a flag, or **beamed** in groups.

Each has a matching **rest** — a silence of the same length. Rests are as important as notes: the music keeps counting through them.

**Counting quavers:** "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and".

**Clap before you play — every time.** Clapping the rhythm first separates the two problems: *when* notes happen and *which* notes. Count aloud while clapping; then play on one open string; then add the fingers.

**Rhythm and the bow:** on the violin, longer notes need **slower bow speed** (or less bow) so you do not run out. A crotchet and a minim in one bow need different speeds. Plan where in the bow you will be.

**Dotted notes:** a dot adds **half the note's value** — a dotted minim is 3 beats; a dotted crotchet is 1½ beats.

Practise with a metronome at 60 bpm; speed up only when it is steady and the rests are full length.

## Key words

- **Crotchet:** a quarter note — one beat
- **Quaver:** an eighth note — half a beat
- **Rest:** a written silence of a set length
- **Dotted note:** a note lengthened by half its value

lessons.summary: Taking a tune you already know by ear and finding it on the instrument.
objectives: You will find a familiar tune by ear in first position

You will play it with a steady pulse
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Choose a melody the class knows and hum it first
- Find the first three notes by ear, then the rest
- Write down what you found and play it back

## Understand it

Playing **by ear** — finding a tune you know without written music — is one of the most useful skills a musician can have, and much traditional and popular music has always been passed on that way.

**How to find a melody by ear:**

1. **Sing or hum it** first, many times, until you know it exactly. If you cannot sing it, you cannot find it.
2. Find the **first note** — try notes until one matches what you sing.
3. For each next note ask: does it go **up or down**? **A little or a lot**? Then try the nearest notes in that direction.
4. Work in **short phrases** — three or four notes at a time — and repeat each phrase until it is secure before going on.
5. Notice **patterns**: repeated phrases, a phrase that moves up step by step, a leap to a high note.

**Choosing the key:** many melodies fit easily in **A major** or **D major** on the violin. If you find a note that needs a fingering you do not know, try starting the tune on a different note.

Nigerian melodies — church choruses, folk songs, highlife tunes and popular songs — often use the **pentatonic scale** (five notes) and **call-and-response** patterns, where a leader's phrase is answered by a group phrase. Look for those shapes.

Once found, **write it down** — note names or notation — so you keep it.

## Key words

- **Playing by ear:** finding music by listening rather than reading
- **Melody:** a tune — a sequence of single notes
- **Call and response:** a phrase answered by another phrase
- **Pentatonic scale:** a scale of five notes

lessons.title: Intonation: going back over earlier weeks
lessons.summary: Returning to the week 3 scale and the week 6 tune with a tuner, and fixing what has drifted.
objectives: You will check an earlier scale against a tuner
You will name your two least reliable notes
You will fix one of them
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play the week 3 A major scale again, stopping on each note with a tuner
- Write down which two notes are consistently sharp or flat
- Drill only those two notes for ten minutes

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys A B C#5 D5 E5 F#5 G#5
```

## Understand it

**Intonation** — playing in tune — is a lifelong study for every violinist. Unlike piano or guitar, nothing fixes the pitch; the ear must check every note. Going back to the week 3 scale with a tuner shows exactly where your hand has learnt the shape and where it has not.

**The exercise:**

1. Play the **A major scale** slowly, **stopping on each note**.
2. Check it on a **tuner** (a free app is fine): is the needle centred, or sharp (too high) or flat (too low)?
3. If it is out, **move the finger** — do not just accept it. Then play it again and memorise the feel of the correct place.
4. Write down **which two notes are most often out**. For most beginners it is the **2nd finger (C♯ and G♯)** — too low, not close enough to the 3rd.

**Using the ear, not only the tuner:**

- **Ringing tones**: some notes make the open strings vibrate in sympathy when perfectly in tune (D on the A string with open D; A on the E string with open A). Listen for the extra resonance.
- Play the note against an **open string** (a **double stop**) and listen for a smooth sound without "beats" (wobbling).
- **Sing** the scale and then play it — the voice trains the ear.

The tuner checks; the ear must eventually do the job alone.

## Key words

- **Sharp / flat (out of tune):** slightly too high / too low
- **Tuner:** a device showing whether a pitch is in tune
- **Sympathetic resonance:** an open string vibrating when a matching note is played
- **Double stop:** two strings played together

lessons.title: Slurs and sharing the bow
lessons.summary: Two or more notes in one bow, and planning where the bow runs out.
objectives: You will play two notes in one bow
You will plan bowing for a four-bar phrase
You will say why bow distribution matters
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play the A scale two notes to a bow, then four
- Mark a phrase with up-bow and down-bow signs
- Play a long note using the whole bow evenly

## Understand it

A **slur** — a curved line over or under two or more different notes — means **play them in one bow**, without changing direction. Slurs make phrases smooth and connected (**legato**), like singing.

**How to slur:**

- The bow keeps moving in the same direction; only the **left-hand fingers** change the notes.
- **Divide the bow**: if you play four notes in one bow, each gets about a quarter of the bow. Plan the bow speed so you do not run out before the slur ends.
- When the slur crosses strings, the **bow arm changes level smoothly** — the elbow leads.

(Do not confuse a slur with a **tie** — a curve joining two notes of the **same pitch**, which become one longer note.)

**Bow markings:**

- ⊓ = **down-bow** (frog to tip); V = **up-bow** (tip to frog).
- In most music, the **strong beat** (beat 1) is played **down-bow**, because down-bows naturally sound stronger. Planning bowings so this works is called **bow distribution**.

**Exercise:** play the A major scale **two notes to a bow**, then **four**, then the whole octave up in one bow and down in one bow — a real test of bow control. Keep the sound even through every note.

Orchestras mark matching bowings in every part so all violins move together — that is why sections look so tidy.

## Key words

- **Slur:** several notes played in one bow
- **Legato:** smooth and connected
- **Tie:** a curve joining two notes of the same pitch into one
- **Bow distribution:** planning how much bow each note uses

lessons.title: D major, and the second finger pattern
lessons.summary: A second scale, and the half-step that moves when the key changes.
objectives: You will play a one-octave D major scale
You will show where the second finger moves between A and D major
You will play a tune in D
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play D major from the open D string
- Compare the second finger in D major with A major — it moves
- Play a short tune in D

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys D E F# G A B C#5
```

```keys A B C#5 D5 E5 F#5 G#5
```

## Understand it

**D major** — D E F♯ G A B C♯ D — starts on the **open D string** and is one of the easiest and most common keys for the violin.

**On the D string:** open **D**, 1 → **E**, 2 → **F♯**, 3 → **G**. Then on the A string: open **A**, 1 → **B**, 2 → **C♯**, 3 → **D**.

Notice: on both strings the **2nd finger is placed high, close to the 3rd** (F♯ and C♯). This is the same **"2–3 pattern"** you used for A major — the pattern T T S (tone, tone, semitone) repeats for the bottom four notes of each half of the scale.

**Comparing with A major:** in A major you played this pattern on the A and E strings; in D major, on the D and A strings. **Same hand shape, different strings** — the violin's fingerboard is **tuned in fifths**, so a pattern moved one string across moves the scale up or down a fifth.

**Other finger patterns:** when the 2nd finger sits **low**, close to the 1st (as for C natural on the A string, or F natural on the D string), it is the **1–2 pattern**. Learning to switch between high 2 and low 2 is the key to playing in many keys.

**Practise:** D major slowly with a tuner, then a simple tune in D. Listen to the **F♯** — it is often played too low.

## Key words

- **D major:** a scale with two sharps, F♯ and C♯
- **Tuned in fifths:** each string five notes above the next
- **High 2 / low 2:** second finger placed near the third / near the first

lessons.title: Tone and dynamics
lessons.summary: Changing volume with bow speed, weight and where you bow, instead of just pressing harder.
objectives: You will play the same note loudly and softly with good tone
You will name the three things that change volume
You will shape a phrase
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play one long note quiet to loud and back, keeping it clean
- Change volume with bow speed, then with weight, then with contact point
- Shape a four-bar phrase: grow to the third bar, ease off

## Understand it

On the violin, **dynamics** and **tone colour** come almost entirely from the bow arm. The three controls:

1. **Bow speed** — faster bow = louder (and brighter); slower bow = softer.
2. **Bow weight** — more arm weight into the string = louder, fuller; less = softer.
3. **Contact point** — closer to the bridge = louder, more brilliant and focused (needs more weight and slower bow); closer to the fingerboard = softer, sweeter, airier (lighter weight, faster bow).

To get louder, you usually change **all three together**: more weight, more speed, contact point nearer the bridge.

**The exercise — one long note, *messa di voce*:** start very soft, grow to loud, return to soft, all in **one bow** (or one down and one up). Keep the sound **clean** — no crunching as it grows, no whistle as it fades. This is one of the oldest exercises for string players and singers.

**Vibrato** — the gentle wobble in pitch that gives violin its warmth — comes later, once intonation is secure.

**Dynamics in music:** *pp, p, mp, mf, f, ff*, and the hairpins **<** (crescendo) and **>** (diminuendo). Mark them in your music in pencil and plan which part of the bow each will use.

A phrase that grows and fades sounds alive; one at a single volume sounds mechanical.

## Key words

- **Bow weight:** arm weight transferred into the string
- **Messa di voce:** a long note that swells and fades
- **Vibrato:** a slight regular change in pitch for warmth
- **Hairpin:** a < or > sign for getting louder or softer

lessons.title: Playing in two parts
lessons.summary: Holding your own line while somebody else plays a different one.
objectives: You will play a second part against a melody
You will stay in time with another player
You will tune to another instrument
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Tune to the open A of another player or a piano
- Play a simple two-part round, swapping parts
- Listen more than you play — match their tone and tempo

## Understand it

Playing in an ensemble — a duet, a string group, a church orchestra — means **listening to others while playing yourself**. It is a different skill from playing alone, and the most rewarding.

**Tune together first.** Orchestras tune to an **A** (usually from the oboe or a piano), at **A = 440 Hz**. Tune your **A string** to it, then tune each other string by playing **two open strings together** (A with D, D with G, A with E) and listening for a smooth, steady sound. When two strings are a perfect fifth apart, they "lock"; when slightly out, the sound **beats** (wobbles).

**Rounds** are the best first ensemble music: everyone plays the same melody, but each part starts a few bars after the last. Simple to learn, and you must hold your part against what others are playing.

**Ensemble skills:**

- **Count** — never get lost; count rests out loud in your head.
- **Listen** — is your part the melody (play out) or accompaniment (play under)?
- **Breathe and start together** — watch the leader, who gives the upbeat with the bow or a nod.
- **Match** — dynamics, bowings and note lengths, so the group sounds like one instrument.
- **Keep going** if you go wrong — find your place and come back in.

**Swap parts.** Playing the other line helps you understand how your part fits.

## Key words

- **Ensemble:** a group of musicians playing together
- **A = 440:** the standard tuning pitch for A
- **Round:** the same melody started at different times by different parts
- **Beats (tuning):** the wobble heard when two notes are slightly out of tune

lessons.title: Term recital
lessons.summary: Performing a prepared piece from memory in front of an audience.
objectives: You will perform a prepared piece from memory
You will tune before you start
You will recover from a mistake without stopping
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Tune, settle, breathe, then start — do not rush the beginning
- Perform your piece
- Give one useful note to two classmates

## Understand it

A recital is a short, finished performance — the same skill professional musicians use on every stage.

**Preparing:**

- Choose a piece that is **secure** — slightly easier than your limit, so nerves do not push it over.
- Mark your music: bowings, fingerings, dynamics, breath points between phrases.
- Practise **performing**, not only practising: play straight through without stopping, even after mistakes, several times — ideally to family or friends.
- Practise the **first and last phrases** most.

**On the day:**

1. **Tune carefully** — check each string; tune again just before you play (strings move with temperature and handling).
2. **Warm up**: long slow bows on open strings, a scale.
3. **Settle**: feet steady, violin up, bow on the string. **Breathe** out slowly.
4. **Hear the first bars in your head** at the right tempo before you start. Do not rush the beginning — nerves make everything faster.

**During:** play to the end; if you slip, keep the pulse and rejoin. **Phrase** — grow and fade, shape each line.

**After:** bow to the audience; it is part of the performance. Then give **one honest piece of feedback to a classmate** — one specific strength and one specific suggestion. Learning to listen and describe others' playing sharpens your own ear.

## Key words

- **Recital:** a short formal performance
- **Phrasing:** shaping music into musical sentences
- **Stage nerves:** the adrenaline of performing, which preparation controls

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize
- [Violin: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/violin/) — Yamaha

## Practise at home

1. Run the piece from the start daily, including the walk-on
1. Practise carrying on after a deliberate mistake

lessons.title: Putting it together, and your first sound
lessons.summary: Assembling the instrument, fitting the reed, and making a steady note.
objectives: You will assemble the saxophone safely
You will fit a reed so it is level with the tip
You will produce a steady note
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Assemble neck, mouthpiece and reed — never force a joint
- Soak the reed, line its tip level with the mouthpiece tip, tighten the ligature gently
- Blow a steady note on the mouthpiece alone first

## Understand it

The saxophone was invented by **Adolphe Sax** in Belgium in the 1840s. Although it is made of brass, it is a **woodwind** instrument, because the sound comes from a **reed** vibrating against a **mouthpiece** — like a clarinet. It is central to jazz, highlife, Afrobeat (Fela played tenor and alto saxophone), gospel and pop.

The common types: **soprano**, **alto** (the usual beginner instrument), **tenor** and **baritone**.

**Assembling — gently:**

1. **Neck strap** on first, so the instrument is supported before you hold it.
2. **Neck into body** — loosen the screw, twist the neck in gently; **never force** a joint or bend the long rod on the neck (the octave mechanism).
3. **Mouthpiece onto the cork** of the neck — twisting on, about halfway down the cork (cork grease if it is tight).
4. **Reed** — wet it in your mouth or a cup of water for a minute. Place the flat side against the mouthpiece, **tip level with the mouthpiece tip** (a hair below is fine), centred.
5. **Ligature** over it, screws tightened just enough to hold the reed.

**Embouchure** (mouth shape):

- Bottom lip slightly **over the lower teeth**, cushioning the reed.
- **Top teeth rest on top** of the mouthpiece (about 1–1.5 cm from the tip).
- Corners of the mouth firm, sealing around it like a drawstring.

**First sound:** breathe deeply and blow steadily on the mouthpiece and neck alone. Aim for a clear, steady note, not a squeak.

## Key words

- **Reed:** a thin cane strip that vibrates to make the sound
- **Ligature:** the clamp that holds the reed on the mouthpiece
- **Embouchure:** the shape and use of the mouth on the mouthpiece
- **Woodwind:** instruments sounded by a reed or by blowing across an edge

## Read and watch

- [Saxophone: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/saxophone/) — Yamaha
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Mouthpiece alone, five long steady notes a day
1. Assemble and pack away the instrument twice a day until it is automatic

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Hold each note for four slow counts before joining them up. One clean note is the whole skill.
- **If you already can:** Play it an octave up, then improvise two bars of your own over the same chords.

lessons.title: Your first three notes: B, A, G
lessons.summary: The three notes every saxophone method starts with, and the fingers that make them.
objectives: You will finger B, A and G
You will move between them without stopping the air
You will hold each for four counts
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Finger B (one finger), A (two), G (three) — left hand only
- Play B-A-G-A-B slowly, keeping the air going
- Keep the embouchure still while the fingers move

## Understand it

The first notes on the saxophone use only the **left hand**, which sits at the **top** of the instrument. (The right hand rests at the bottom, thumb under the thumb rest, fingers lightly over the lower keys.)

**Left hand position:** thumb on the thumb rest at the back (next to the **octave key**); index, middle and ring fingers on the **three main keys** (the pearl buttons) on the front.

**The first three notes:**

- **B** — first finger only.
- **A** — first and second fingers.
- **G** — first, second and third fingers.

**Tips:**

- **Pads of the fingers** on the pearls, fingers gently curved, close to the keys.
- Press keys **fully and together** — half-pressed keys leak air and give squeaks or wrong notes.
- Do not touch the side keys with your palm — that opens extra holes.

**Play B–A–G–A–B slowly**, holding each note for four beats. Listen to keep the tone **the same on every note** — beginners often let G go weak or airy. Keep the air **steady and supported** as fingers change; the fingers move, the air does not stop.

These three notes are enough to play many simple tunes — which is a good reason to learn them really well.

## Key words

- **Pearl keys:** the main finger buttons on the front of the sax
- **Octave key:** a thumb key that raises notes an octave
- **Fingering:** which keys to press for a note

- [Saxophone: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/saxophone/) — Yamaha

lessons.title: Breathing and long tones
lessons.summary: Where the air comes from, and the exercise that builds every other thing.
objectives: You will breathe from the stomach, not the shoulders
You will hold a note for eight slow counts
You will keep the volume even through it
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Breathe with a hand on your stomach — it should move out, shoulders still
- Long tones: one note, eight counts, even all the way
- Do them on G, A and B

## Understand it

Every wind player's tone depends on **breath support** — a steady, controlled stream of air from deep in the body. Without it, the sound is thin, wobbly and out of tune, however good the fingers.

**Breathing low:**

- Put a hand on your stomach. Breathe in through the mouth (around the mouthpiece corners): the **stomach and lower ribs expand outwards**, the **shoulders stay still**.
- Shoulders rising means you are breathing high in the chest — that gives less air and creates tension.
- Breathing out, keep the abdominal muscles **engaged**, pushing the air out steadily — like blowing a long, steady stream to keep a candle flame bent but not out.

**Long tones** — the most important exercise for all wind players:

1. Choose a comfortable note (G, A or B).
2. Hold it for as long as you can with a **steady, even, full sound** — aim for 8, then 12, then 16 counts at 60 bpm.
3. Listen: does the pitch stay steady (check with a tuner)? Does the volume stay level? Does the tone stay clear to the very end?
4. Rest, breathe, repeat on other notes.

Long tones build breath control, embouchure strength and tone. Professional players do them every day as a warm-up. Five minutes a day makes a bigger difference than an hour once a week.

## Key words

- **Breath support:** steady controlled air from the abdominal muscles
- **Long tones:** holding notes steadily to build tone and control
- **Diaphragm:** the muscle under the lungs used in deep breathing

- [Saxophone: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/saxophone/) — Yamaha
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Ten long tones a day. This is the exercise that matters most
1. Breathe in for four, out for eight, away from the instrument

lessons.title: The C major scale
lessons.summary: One octave of C major, and the fingerings you have not met yet.
objectives: You will play a one-octave C major scale
You will name every note in it
You will play it up and down evenly
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn the new fingerings between G and C
- Play the scale slowly, four counts a note, then two, then one
- Say the note names out loud as you play

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it to explain an alternative fingering, then test it at the instrument against the one you were taught. Your ears decide, not the answer.

## Understand it

The **C major scale** — C D E F G A B C — has no sharps or flats; it is the reference all others are compared with.

**Saxophones are transposing instruments.** The alto saxophone is pitched in **E♭**: when you play a written C, the sound is actually an E♭. Tenor saxophone is in **B♭**. This lets saxophonists use the same fingerings on every sax, but it means your **written** C major is a different **concert** key from a piano's C major. When playing with a pianist or band, you must agree which key — "written" or "concert". (For now: play from music written for your saxophone.)

**Fingerings, from written low C up:**

- **C** — all six main keys (left hand B A G + right hand F E D) plus the low C key with the right little finger.
- **D** — all six main keys.
- **E** — left hand three + right hand first and second.
- **F** — left hand three + right hand first.
- **G, A, B** — left hand three, two, one.
- **C** (middle) — left hand **second finger** only.

**Practising:** slowly, **four counts a note**, then two, then one. Keep the air steady and the tone even across every note; low notes need **more air and a more relaxed throat**. Watch for **finger coordination** where several fingers move at once (C to D, B to C) — they must move together.

## Key words

- **Transposing instrument:** one whose written notes sound at a different pitch
- **Concert pitch:** the actual sounding pitch, as on a piano
- **E♭ alto:** the alto sax sounds a sixth below written notes

lessons.title: Tonguing
lessons.summary: Starting a note with the tongue instead of the throat, and the difference it makes.
objectives: You will start a note with the tip of the tongue
You will play four tongued notes and four slurred
You will say what legato and staccato mean
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Say "too" to find where the tongue touches the reed
- Play four tongued, four slurred, on one note
- Apply it to the C major scale

## See it and hear it

Press **Hear it** under a diagram to play it, note by note.

```keys C D E F G A B
```

## Understand it

**Tonguing** starts each note cleanly — like the consonant at the start of a word. Without it, notes just blur into each other (slurring) or start with a messy "huh" of breath.

**How it works:**

- Say the syllable **"too"** or **"doo"**. Notice where your tongue touches: just behind the top teeth.
- On the saxophone, the **tip of the tongue lightly touches the tip of the reed**. Air pressure builds behind it.
- The tongue **releases** — "too" — and the reed starts to vibrate.
- **The air keeps flowing.** The tongue does not stop the air; it briefly interrupts the reed. Think of it as a tap, not a stop.

**Common faults:**

- Tongue hitting too hard → explosive "thud".
- Moving the jaw → the pitch wobbles.
- Stopping the air between notes → choppy, weak tone.

**Slurred vs tongued:**

- **Slurred** — one breath and only the first note tongued; fingers change the notes. Smooth.
- **Tongued** — every note started with the tongue. Clear and separated.
- Music marks slurs with curves; the notes under a curve are slurred.

**Exercise:** on one note, four tongued crotchets, then four slurred (changing notes); then mix. Start slowly. Later: **staccato** (short, detached) notes, marked with a dot.

## Key words

- **Tonguing:** starting a note with the tongue on the reed
- **Articulation:** how notes are started, joined or separated
- **Slur:** notes played in one breath without tonguing
- **Staccato:** short, detached notes

## Read and watch

- [Saxophone: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/saxophone/) — Yamaha
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

1. Four tongued notes on each note of the scale

lessons.title: Playing a tune
lessons.summary: Putting the scale, the tonguing and the breathing into a real melody.
objectives: You will play an eight-bar melody
You will breathe at the end of phrases, not in the middle
You will play it with a steady pulse
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn an eight-bar melody the class chooses
- Mark where you will breathe before you play
- Play it with a metronome at a slow tempo

## Understand it

A tune puts your notes, breath and tonguing together into music. The new challenge is **breathing in the right places**.

**Plan your breaths before you play.** Wind players breathe at the **ends of phrases** — the natural pauses, like commas and full stops in speech. Breathing in the middle of a phrase breaks the musical sentence; not planning means running out of air at the worst moment.

- Mark breaths in pencil with a tick (**✓**) or comma above the stave.
- Breathe **quickly and deeply** — the breath takes time from the note before, not the note after.
- Shorter phrases (four bars) are easier at first; aim for eight.

**Learning an eight-bar melody:**

1. **Listen** to it and **sing** it.
2. Clap the rhythm.
3. Finger it without blowing.
4. Play each **two-bar** section slowly, then join them.
5. Add **tonguing and slurs** as written.
6. Increase the tempo only when it is clean.

**Phrasing:** a phrase usually grows towards its most important note (often the highest or longest) and relaxes at the end. Even at one dynamic, this shape makes a melody sing.

Play along with a recording or backing track when you can — it trains you to keep time and stay in tune with others.

## Key words

- **Phrase:** a musical sentence, often four or eight bars
- **Breath mark:** a tick or comma showing where to breathe
- **Phrasing:** shaping a phrase towards and away from its peak

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize
- [Music theory lessons](https://www.musictheory.net/lessons) — musictheory.net

lessons.summary: Returning to the week 3 long tones and the week 4 scale, and hearing what has changed.
objectives: You will record and listen back to an earlier exercise

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Record the week 3 long tones again and compare with how they sounded then
- Play the week 4 scale and mark the note with the worst tone
- Drill that one note for ten minutes

## Understand it

Tone is the saxophonist's voice — the first thing listeners notice. Comparing recordings across weeks shows your progress more honestly than memory.

**The exercise:**

1. Record your **long tones** (week 3 notes) again, on the same phone in the same room.
2. Play the **C major scale** (week 4) and record it.
3. Listen back **next to the earlier recordings**.

**What to listen for:**

- **Steadiness** — does the note hold without wobbling in pitch or volume?
- **Fullness** — rich and round, or thin and airy?
- **Evenness across the scale** — do low notes speak clearly? Do some notes stick out as different in colour?
- **Pitch** — check with a tuner. **Sharp** notes often come from **biting** (pressing the jaw too hard on the reed); **flat** notes from a loose embouchure or weak air.
- **Starts** — clean tonguing, or a puff of air first?

**Equipment checks** affect tone too:

- **Reed** — chipped, warped or too soft reeds squeak and buzz. Rotate between two or three reeds and store them flat.
- **Leaks** — a pad not sealing (often from a bent key) makes low notes impossible. Ask your instructor to check.

Write down **one specific fix** and work on it with long tones every day.

## Key words

- **Tone:** the quality or colour of the sound
- **Biting:** pressing too hard on the reed with the jaw
- **Leak:** a pad that does not seal, letting air escape

- [Saxophone: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/saxophone/) — Yamaha

lessons.title: The octave key
lessons.summary: Opening the upper register, and keeping the tone when you go up.
objectives: You will play the octave above your first notes
You will use the octave key with the left thumb
You will keep the embouchure steady across the break
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play low G, then G with the octave key — same fingers
- Work through the scale an octave up
- Do not bite — the embouchure stays the same

## Understand it

The **octave key** — pressed with the **left thumb** — opens a small hole that makes the saxophone sound **one octave higher** with the **same fingering**. Low G with the octave key becomes the G above it. This doubles your range with very little new fingering to learn.

**Making the upper notes work:**

- **Same fingers**, add the thumb by **rolling** it onto the octave key — do not lift the thumb off the thumb rest area completely.
- **Steady, fast air** — upper notes need faster, more focused air, like aiming further.
- **Do not bite** — the natural tendency is to tighten the jaw to reach up; it makes notes sharp and thin. Keep the embouchure firm at the corners, not pinched.
- **Voicing** — the shape inside your mouth matters: think of the tongue position for "ee" for upper notes, "aw" for lower ones.

**Exercises:**

1. Play low **G**, then G **with the octave key** — same fingers. Let the jump happen without moving the mouth.
2. Work up the scale: low D → high D, E → high E, and so on.
3. **Slur octaves** (low to high in one breath) — the hardest and most useful.

**Middle D** (the first note with the octave key and all fingers down) is often the trickiest — it can crack or warble. Long tones on it help.

With the octave key, you can play a full **two-octave** range for most tunes.

## Key words

- **Octave:** the same note eight notes higher or lower
- **Octave key:** the thumb key that raises a note by an octave
- **Voicing:** the shape inside the mouth that helps notes speak

lessons.title: Highlife and Afrobeat lines
lessons.summary: The riffs and horn lines that the saxophone plays in Nigerian music.
objectives: You will play a highlife horn riff
You will play it in time with a groove
You will name two Nigerian saxophonists
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Listen to a highlife or Afrobeat horn line and sing it first
- Learn it by ear, four bars at a time
- Play it over a backing groove

## Understand it

Nigerian popular music has given the saxophone some of its great roles.

**Highlife** began in Ghana and spread across West Africa in the early twentieth century, mixing local rhythms and melodies with brass band and dance band music. Nigerian highlife bandleaders such as **Bobby Benson**, **Victor Olaiya** and **Rex Lawson** led bands with horn sections — saxophones and trumpets playing catchy melodies in harmony.

**Afrobeat** — **Fela Kuti** (who played saxophone himself), with **Tony Allen** on drums — used big horn sections playing **riffs**: short, repeated, punchy phrases that lock with the groove, often answering the vocals.

**Learning lines by ear** — the way most horn players in these traditions learnt:

1. **Listen** many times. Choose a short section — four bars.
2. **Sing it**. If you can sing it accurately, you can find it.
3. **Find the first note** on the saxophone, then each next one by going up or down.
4. Copy the **feel** as well as the notes: the **articulation** (short, punchy notes vs smooth ones), the accents, how notes are placed against the beat (often slightly **behind**, relaxed).
5. Repeat each section until secure, then join sections.

Use a phone app to **slow recordings down** without changing the pitch.

Notice **call and response** — the horns answering the singer — a structure that runs through West African music.

## Key words

- **Highlife:** West African dance band music with horn melodies
- **Riff:** a short repeated musical phrase
- **Horn section:** a group of brass and saxophone players
- **Call and response:** a phrase answered by another

## Read and watch

- [Search: highlife](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=highlife) — Google Arts & Culture
- [Search: Fela Kuti](https://artsandculture.google.com/search?q=fela%20kuti) — Google Arts & Culture

## Practise at home

1. The riff daily, with a drum track or a metronome
1. Learn one more riff by ear this week

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Hold each note for four slow counts before joining them up. One clean note is the whole skill.
- **If you already can:** Play it an octave up, then improvise two bars of your own over the same chords.

## Assessed this week

**Practical (6 marks) —** Play a four-bar horn riff from memory, in time with a groove.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.
