lessons.title: Dynamics and phrasing
lessons.summary: Shaping a line rather than playing it flat, and changing volume without changing pitch.
objectives: You will play a phrase with a shape
You will change volume while keeping the note in tune
You will say where a phrase should grow and ease off
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play one note quiet to loud and back, watching the tuner
- Shape an eight-bar phrase: grow to bar five, ease off at the end
- Play the week 6 tune with a shape

## Understand it

**Dynamics** on the saxophone come from **air speed and quantity**, while the embouchure keeps the pitch steady. This is harder than it sounds: when you play louder, the pitch tends to go **flat**; softer, it goes **sharp** — so you must adjust while changing volume.

**The exercise:** one long note, growing from very soft (**pp**) to loud (**f**) and back, watching the tuner. Keep the needle centred:

- Going **louder** — more air, keep the jaw firm (not dropping), corners firm.
- Going **softer** — less air but **keep it supported and fast** (soft does not mean weak); do not pinch.

Soft playing is the harder skill. A good player can play quietly with a clear tone and in tune.

**Shaping a phrase:**

- Find the **peak** — the most important note (often the highest or longest).
- **Grow** towards it (crescendo), **relax** after it (diminuendo).
- **Taper the ends of phrases** — do not stop the note abruptly; let it fade naturally.

Mark your plan in pencil: *p* at the start, a crescendo hairpin to the peak, a diminuendo after.

**Expression** — combining dynamics, articulation (tongued, slurred, accented) and tone colour — is what makes a melody speak. Listen to how great saxophonists shape a ballad; the notes are simple, but every note has a direction.

## Key words

- **Dynamics:** the loudness and softness of music
- **Taper:** letting a note fade smoothly at the end
- **Expression:** shaping music with dynamics, articulation and tone

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize
- [Saxophone: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/saxophone/) — Yamaha

## Practise at home

1. Quiet-to-loud long tones, five a day, checking the tuner
1. Play the tune twice: once flat, once shaped, and hear the difference

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Hold each note for four slow counts before joining them up. One clean note is the whole skill.
- **If you already can:** Play it an octave up, then improvise two bars of your own over the same chords.

## Assessed this week

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Playing with a band
lessons.summary: Coming in on the right beat, matching the horn section, and knowing when not to play.
objectives: You will count yourself in and enter on the right beat
You will match another player's tuning and volume
You will stay silent where the part is silent
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Tune to the band before anything else
- Count four bars of rest and come in exactly
- Play a line in unison with another horn and match them

## Understand it

In a band, the saxophone's job changes: you play a **part**, which must fit with everyone else.

**Tune first.** Bands tune to a **concert B♭** or **concert A**, given by a keyboard or tuner. On alto saxophone (in E♭), concert B♭ is your written **G**; concert A is your written **F♯**. Adjust the **mouthpiece on the cork** — push in to raise the pitch, pull out to lower it. Warm up first: a cold instrument plays flat.

**Count and come in exactly.** Horn parts often have many bars of rest. **Count every bar** ("1-2-3-4, 2-2-3-4, 3-2-3-4…") and watch for cues. Coming in a beat early or late is very obvious with horns.

**Play your part in style:**

- **Riffs and backing lines** — short, tight, together with the other horns.
- **Balance** — when the singer is singing, **play under** them; you are accompaniment. Play out only on your melody or solo.
- **Match** articulation and note lengths with the other horn players; agree whether notes are short or long.

**Listening** is the core skill: to the drums and bass for time, to the other horns for tuning and blend, to the singer for when to play softer.

**Concert keys:** with a band you will often hear songs named in concert keys — an alto player transposes up a **major sixth** (or down a minor third) to find their written key. Ask the band leader or use parts written for alto.

## Key words

- **Concert B♭:** the band's tuning note — written G on alto sax
- **Part:** the music one instrument plays in an ensemble
- **Balance:** the right volume of each part so all are heard properly
- **Entry:** coming in after rests

## Read and watch

- [Saxophone: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/saxophone/) — Yamaha
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Practise your entry against a recording — count the bars aloud
1. Play the riff along with the record, matching its volume

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Hold each note for four slow counts before joining them up. One clean note is the whole skill.
- **If you already can:** Play it an octave up, then improvise two bars of your own over the same chords.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Term performance
lessons.summary: Playing a prepared piece with a shaped phrase and a clean ending.
objectives: You will perform a prepared piece
You will tune and warm up before playing
You will give a classmate one useful note
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Warm up with long tones, tune, then perform
- Play your piece with planned breaths and a shaped phrase
- Listen to two classmates and give each one note

## Understand it

Your term performance pulls everything together: **tone, breath, tonguing, dynamics and phrasing** in one finished piece.

**Preparing:**

- Choose a piece that is **secure** at the tempo you will play it.
- Mark breaths, dynamics and articulation in pencil — and practise them every time, not only on the day.
- Practise **performing**: straight through, without stopping for mistakes.
- **Choose your reed** in advance — one that has played well for a few days, not a brand-new one. Bring a spare.

**On the day:**

1. **Warm up** with long tones — they settle the breath and the embouchure.
2. **Tune** to the piano or tuner after warming up.
3. Before starting, take a **calm, low breath**, think the tempo, and begin.

**During:** plan your breaths and take them; shape each phrase towards its peak; **keep going** if a note cracks or squeaks — the audience forgets quickly if you do not react.

**After:** clean the instrument — **swab** the body and neck to remove moisture, wipe the mouthpiece, store the reed flat in a reed case. Moisture left in damages the pads.

**Reflect:** listen to a recording. What improved this term? What is the one thing to work on next (often: soft playing, low notes, or tonguing speed)? Write it down so next term starts with a goal.

## Key words

- **Swab:** a cloth pulled through the instrument to dry it
- **Reed case:** a holder that keeps reeds flat and safe
- **Performance practice:** rehearsing as if performing — without stopping

## Read and watch

- [Saxophone: musical instrument guide](https://www.yamaha.com/en/musical_instrument_guide/saxophone/) — Yamaha
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Run the piece from the top daily, including the ending
1. Practise carrying on after a deliberate mistake

## Make it fit you

lessons.title: Your voice is an instrument
lessons.summary: How the voice actually works, how to stand, and why the breath is the whole thing.
objectives: You will stand in a balanced singing posture
You will breathe low without lifting your shoulders
You will say what the vocal folds do
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Stand with feet apart, knees soft, head level — not chin up
- Hand on the stomach: breathe in so the hand moves out
- Hiss on one long breath and time it

## Understand it

Your voice is a real instrument, with three parts working together:

1. **The power source — breath.** The lungs supply air, controlled by the **diaphragm** (a dome-shaped muscle under the lungs) and the abdominal and rib muscles.
2. **The vibrator — the vocal folds** (often called vocal cords): two small folds of tissue in the **larynx** (voice box, in the throat). Air from the lungs makes them vibrate hundreds of times a second, creating the sound. Faster vibration = higher pitch.
3. **The resonators — throat, mouth and nose.** They amplify and colour the sound, like the body of a guitar. Changing their shape changes the vowel and the tone.

**Posture** lets all three work freely:

- Feet apart (hip width), weight even, **knees soft** (not locked).
- Spine long, shoulders relaxed and down.
- **Head level** — not chin up (which squeezes the larynx) or tucked down.

**Breathing for singing:**

- Hand on the stomach. Breathe in: the **stomach and lower ribs move outwards**; shoulders and chest stay still.
- Breathe out on a hiss ("sss") slowly and evenly — aim for 20 seconds, then 30.

High, shallow "shoulder breathing" gives little air and makes the throat tense. Low breathing gives a steady, supported sound — the foundation for everything else in this course.

## Key words

- **Vocal folds:** the two folds in the larynx that vibrate to make sound
- **Larynx:** the voice box, in the throat
- **Diaphragm:** the breathing muscle under the lungs
- **Resonance:** the amplifying and colouring of sound in the throat, mouth and nose

## Read and watch

- [Taking care of your voice](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/taking-care-your-voice) — US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Low breathing for three minutes a day, lying down if easier
1. Time your hiss daily and watch the number grow

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work at a comfortable volume in the middle of your range. Pushing a tired voice makes it worse, not stronger.
- **If you already can:** Sing it in a second key, add a harmony line, and record both to compare.

Your instructor watches you do it and marks against this week's three objectives, two marks each. The written check below is worth one mark: this is a practical subject and it is marked like one.

lessons.title: Warming up, and looking after your voice
lessons.summary: The warm-up routine, and the habits that keep a voice working for years.
objectives: You will run a five-minute warm-up unaided
You will name three things that damage a voice
You will stop when something hurts
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Lip trills, humming, sirens, five-note scales
- Learn the rules: water, sleep, no shouting, no singing through pain
- Warm up before every single session from now on

## Understand it

Singers warm up for the same reason athletes do: the vocal folds are muscles and tissue that work better, and are less easily hurt, when gradually prepared.

**A good warm-up (10–15 minutes), from gentle to demanding:**

1. **Body** — shoulder rolls, neck stretches, jaw massage. Release tension.
2. **Breath** — slow low breaths; a long hiss.
3. **Lip trills** ("brrr" with loose lips) or **tongue trills** — gently connect breath and voice with little effort; slide up and down.
4. **Humming** — feel the buzz on the lips and nose.
5. **Sirens** — slide smoothly from low to high and back on "ng" or "oo", like a siren — gently, never forcing the top.
6. **Five-note scales** (1-2-3-4-5-4-3-2-1) on vowels, moving up and down in small steps.

**Looking after your voice:**

- **Water** — drink plenty through the day; the vocal folds need moisture.
- **Sleep** — a tired body gives a tired voice.
- **No shouting or screaming** — at matches, parties, across a playground. It strains and can injure the folds.
- **Do not sing through pain or hoarseness** — rest.
- **Avoid smoke**, and limit throat clearing (it slams the folds together; swallow or sip water instead).
- **Do not whisper to "save" a sore voice** — whispering can strain it too.

**See a doctor** if hoarseness lasts more than about **two to three weeks**.

## Key words

- **Warm-up:** exercises that prepare the voice gradually
- **Lip trill:** blowing through loose lips while voicing, to connect breath and sound
- **Siren:** a smooth slide through the range
- **Vocal hygiene:** habits that keep the voice healthy

## Read and watch

- [Taking care of your voice](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/taking-care-your-voice) — US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

## Practise at home

1. The five-minute warm-up every day, even on days you do not sing
1. Drink water through the day, not just before singing

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work at a comfortable volume in the middle of your range. Pushing a tired voice makes it worse, not stronger.
- **If you already can:** Sing it in a second key, add a harmony line, and record both to compare.

lessons.title: Pitch: matching, and intervals
lessons.summary: Hearing a note and singing the same one, then hearing the distance between two.
objectives: You will match a played note with your voice
You will sing a third, a fourth and a fifth
You will say whether you were sharp or flat
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Match notes played on a keyboard, one at a time
- Sing up a third, fourth, fifth from a given note
- Check yourself on a tuner app

## Understand it

**Pitch** is how high or low a note is. Singing in tune means matching pitches exactly — with the band, the choir, or the recording.

**Pitch matching:**

- Listen to a note from a keyboard or app, **hear it in your head**, then sing it.
- Hum first — humming is easier to tune.
- If you are not sure whether you are too high or too low, **slide** slowly up and down until you lock onto the note — you will hear and feel when it matches.
- Tuner apps show your pitch live, which helps beginners.

**Intervals** are the distances between two notes. Learning to hear and sing them is the key to singing tunes accurately and to harmony. Many singers learn intervals from the start of familiar songs, for example:

- **Major 3rd** — the first two notes of "**Oh When the Saints**" ("Oh — when").
- **Perfect 4th** — "**Here Comes the Bride**".
- **Perfect 5th** — "**Twinkle, twinkle**" (the jump up from the first "twinkle" to the second).
- **Octave** — "**Some-where** over the rainbow".

Find your own examples from songs you know (church songs, Nigerian pop) — they work better because you know them deeply.

**Practise:** play a note, sing up a 3rd, 4th or 5th, then check on the keyboard. Many free ear-training apps and websites drill this.

## Key words

- **Pitch:** how high or low a note is
- **Interval:** the distance between two notes
- **In tune:** matching the intended pitch exactly
- **Ear training:** practice that improves hearing of pitch and intervals

## Read and watch

- [Ear training exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory web](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

## Practise at home

1. Match ten notes a day against a keyboard or app
1. Sing the first interval of two songs you know

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work at a comfortable volume in the middle of your range. Pushing a tired voice makes it worse, not stronger.
- **If you already can:** Sing it in a second key, add a harmony line, and record both to compare.

lessons.title: Resonance: where the sound sits
lessons.summary: Making a bigger sound without pushing harder, by changing where it resonates.
objectives: You will feel resonance in the face and chest
You will sing the same note two ways and hear the difference
You will keep the throat open
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Hum until you feel a buzz in the nose and lips
- Sing "ng" then open to "ah", keeping the buzz
- Yawn-sigh to feel an open throat

## Understand it

**Resonance** is what makes a voice carry, ring and sound full **without** shouting. The vibrations from the vocal folds are amplified in the spaces of the throat, mouth and nasal passages — and singers learn to use those spaces well.

**Feeling resonance:**

- **Hum** on "mm" with your lips closed. You should feel a **buzz** — on the lips, in the nose, in the cheekbones. That buzz is resonance in the front of the face (sometimes called **"the mask"**).
- Sing **"ng"** (as in "sing"), then open slowly to **"ah"** ("nnng-ah"), trying to **keep the buzz** as the mouth opens. The sound should stay bright and forward, not fall back into the throat.

**Why it matters:**

- A resonant voice **carries further** with less effort — it is efficient, not loud.
- It sounds **clearer and richer**.
- It **protects the voice** — pushing for volume from the throat strains it; resonance does the work instead.

**Open space at the back:** a slight **lift of the soft palate** (as at the start of a yawn, or a surprised breath) creates more space in the throat and mouth — a warmer, fuller tone. Keep the jaw **relaxed and dropped**, not clenched.

Different styles use resonance differently: gospel and pop often bright and forward, classical with more space at the back. Most singers balance both.

## Key words

- **Resonance:** amplification of the voice in the throat, mouth and nose
- **Mask:** the front of the face, where forward resonance is felt
- **Soft palate:** the soft back part of the roof of the mouth
- **Placement:** where a singer feels the sound resonate

## Read and watch

- [Taking care of your voice](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/taking-care-your-voice) — US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders
- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

## Practise at home

1. Humming and sirens, five minutes a day
1. Sing one phrase with the buzz, then without, and listen back

## Make it fit you

- **If this is new to you:** Work at a comfortable volume in the middle of your range. Pushing a tired voice makes it worse, not stronger.
- **If you already can:** Sing it in a second key, add a harmony line, and record both to compare.

lessons.summary: Being understood, and knowing what you are actually singing about.
objectives: You will sing consonants clearly without stopping the line
You will say in one sentence what your song is about
You will sing vowels tall and open
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Speak the lyric in rhythm before you sing it
- Exaggerate the consonants, keep the vowels long
- Say what the song means in your own words

. **With an AI assistant —** ask it what a word in your lyric means and how it is pronounced, then check with somebody who speaks the language. It is confident about languages it handles badly.

## Understand it

A song is a **story told in music** — and if the audience cannot understand the words, half the song is lost. **Diction** means clear pronunciation; good singers are understood at the back of the room.

**Vowels and consonants have different jobs:**

- **Vowels carry the sound** — the voice sustains on vowels. Keep them **long, open and pure**, so the tone stays rich ("daaay" not "day-ee").
- **Consonants carry the meaning** — they must be **crisp, quick and clear**, often slightly exaggerated, because they are lost easily over a band or in a large room.
- In a long note, sing the vowel for almost the whole length, then put the final consonant **exactly** at the end ("love": "lu-u-u-v" with the v at the very end).

**Speak it first.** Speak the lyric **in rhythm**, with full meaning, before singing it. You will notice the important words, the natural stresses, where to breathe, and what the line means.

**Languages:** many Nigerian singers sing in English, Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa, Pidgin and others. **Tonal languages** like Yoruba and Igbo create a special challenge: the melody can change a word's tones and so its meaning — songwriters and singers balance the two. When singing in a language you do not speak fluently, learn the meaning and the correct pronunciation from a fluent speaker.

**Meaning shapes delivery** — which word in each line matters most? Lean on it slightly.

## Key words

- **Diction:** clear pronunciation of words in singing
- **Pure vowel:** a vowel held without changing shape
- **Stress:** the emphasis on important syllables and words

lessons.title: Range and the passaggio
lessons.summary: The place where your voice wants to change gear, and how to cross it smoothly.
objectives: You will find where your voice changes quality
You will sing through that point without a break
You will say why you must not force the top
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Sing a slow siren from low to high and mark where it shifts
- Practise five-note scales through that point, lightly
- Never force the top of the range

## Understand it

Your **range** is the span of notes you can sing, from lowest to highest. Most untrained voices cover about an octave and a half; training extends and, more importantly, **evens out** the range.

**Registers:** the voice has different modes of vibration that feel and sound different:

- **Chest voice** — lower notes, felt as vibration in the chest; strong, speech-like.
- **Head voice** — higher notes, felt in the head; lighter, more ringing.
- **Mixed voice (mix)** — a blend, letting singers carry power higher without straining. Pop, gospel and musical theatre singers rely on it.

**The passaggio** (Italian for "passage") is the area where the voice shifts between registers. Untrained singers often **crack** or **flip** there, or **push** the chest voice too high (shouting, straining, going red in the face).

**Smoothing the break:**

- **Sirens** on "ng" or "oo", slowly, through the shift — let it change without forcing.
- **Five-note scales** that cross the passaggio, gently, with **light volume** — volume makes the break worse.
- **Narrow vowels** ("oo", "ee") make crossing easier than wide ones ("ah").
- Keep the **breath steady** and the **jaw and neck relaxed**.

**Never force high notes.** Strain, pain or tightness is a sign to stop. Range grows gradually over months of healthy practice.

## Key words

- **Range:** the span of notes a voice can sing
- **Register:** a mode of the voice — chest, head or mix
- **Passaggio:** the transition area between registers
- **Crack (break):** a sudden flip between registers

## Read and watch

- [Taking care of your voice](https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/taking-care-your-voice) — US National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders

1. Light sirens across the shift, five minutes a day
1. Scales that cross the shift, quietly

lessons.title: Back to week 3: pitch, recorded
lessons.summary: Returning to the interval work of week 3 and measuring it honestly.
objectives: You will record the week 3 intervals again
You will compare the two recordings
You will name the interval you still miss
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Record the same intervals you sang in week 3
- Listen to both recordings side by side
- Drill only the interval you still miss

## Understand it

Our own voices sound different inside our heads (through the bones of the skull) from how others hear them. **Recording** is the only way to hear yourself honestly — and comparing recordings over time shows real progress.

**The exercise:**

1. Record yourself singing the **same intervals** as in week 3, the same way (same phone, same room, same starting note).
2. Listen to both recordings **side by side**.
3. Check each interval against a keyboard or tuner app.

**Questions to ask:**

- Which intervals are **accurately in tune** now?
- Which are still **sharp** (too high) or **flat** (too low)? Most singers have a tendency — often going flat when tired or on descending intervals, or sharp when nervous or pushing.
- Is the **tone** steadier? Does each note start cleanly, or slide in?

**Drilling the weak ones:**

- Play the two notes, **listen**, then sing them.
- **Sing slowly**, holding each note so you can check it.
- Use a **reference song** for each interval.
- Practise a little **every day** — ear training works through frequency.

Do not be discouraged if you dislike how your recorded voice sounds — almost everyone does at first. You will get used to it, and it is the most honest teacher you have.

## Key words

- **Bone conduction:** hearing your voice through your own skull, which changes it
- **Sharp / flat:** slightly too high / too low
- **Self-assessment:** judging your own progress honestly

## Read and watch

- [Ear training exercises](https://www.musictheory.net/exercises) — musictheory.net
- [Music theory web](https://www.teoria.com/) — teoria.com

1. Record again at the end of the week

lessons.title: Singing in parts
lessons.summary: Holding your own line while other people sing different ones.
objectives: You will sing a harmony line against a melody
You will stay on your part when another is louder
You will blend rather than stand out
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Learn a two-part song, swapping parts
- Sing your line while listening to the other
- Match vowels and volume with the people beside you

## Understand it

Singing in **parts** — harmony — is one of the great joys of music, and essential in choirs, church groups and backing vocals.

**Parts in a choir:** **soprano** (highest female), **alto** (lower female), **tenor** (higher male), **bass** (lowest male) — **SATB**. Young singers whose voices have not changed sing soprano or alto.

**The challenge:** keeping your own line while hearing a different one at the same time. Beginners drift onto the melody because it is louder in their ears.

**Skills that help:**

- **Learn your part thoroughly** alone first — until you can sing it confidently without help.
- **Then add the other part quietly**, and gradually louder.
- **Hand over one ear** — hearing yourself more clearly helps you hold your line (choir singers do this in rehearsal).
- **Listen** for how your note fits with the others: when two parts are perfectly in tune, the chord **rings**.
- **Swap parts** — learning the other line shows you how they fit.

**Blend** — sounding like one group, not many soloists:

- **Match vowels** — everyone shapes "ah" the same way.
- **Match volume** — no one sticks out.
- **Start and stop together**, and put final consonants in exactly together.

Rounds ("Frère Jacques" style) are good first part-songs; then simple two-part harmony.

## Key words

- **Harmony:** different notes sung together
- **SATB:** soprano, alto, tenor, bass
- **Blend:** voices matching to sound like one group
- **Round:** the same melody started at different times

## Read and watch

- [GCSE Music](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/subjects/zpf3cdm) — BBC Bitesize

1. Practise your part alone until it is secure

lessons.title: The microphone
lessons.summary: What a microphone does to your voice, and how to work with it.
objectives: You will hold a microphone at the right distance
You will move it for loud and quiet notes
You will avoid feedback
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Hold the mic a hand's width away, pointed at the mouth
- Move it back for loud notes, closer for quiet ones
- Never point the mic at a speaker

## Understand it

A microphone is part of the singer's instrument in almost every modern performance. Good mic technique makes you sound better; poor technique makes you inaudible, distorted or squealing.

**Holding it:**

- Hold it by the **body**, not the head (the grille) — **covering the grille** changes the sound and causes feedback.
- Point it **at your mouth**, about **a hand's width (5–10 cm)** away, for normal singing.
- Keep the distance **consistent** — every time you move it away, you disappear from the mix.

**Working the mic:**

- **Loud or high notes** → move the mic slightly **back**, so the sound does not distort or blast the audience.
- **Soft or intimate passages** → come **closer**, so they are heard.
- **The proximity effect** — dynamic mics (like the Shure SM58) get **bassier** the closer they are. Singers use this for warmth on low notes.
- **Plosives** — "p" and "b" sounds blast air into the mic ("pops"). Sing slightly across the mic rather than straight into it, or turn it a little on those words.

**Feedback** (squealing): never point the mic at a speaker or wave it in front of monitors. If feedback starts, turn the mic away from the speaker.

**Sound check:** sing your **loudest** and **softest** passages for the engineer, at performance volume — not a quiet "one, two".

## Key words

- **Proximity effect:** more bass as a mic gets closer
- **Plosive:** a burst of air from 'p' or 'b' that pops in the mic
- **Feedback:** a squeal when a mic picks up its own speaker
- **Sound check:** testing mic levels before a performance

## Read and watch

- [Audio insights and guides](https://www.shure.com/en-US/insights) — Shure
- [Sound](https://www.theatrecrafts.com/pages/home/topics/sound/) — Theatrecrafts.com

1. Sing one loud and one quiet phrase, adjusting distance

lessons.title: Telling the story
lessons.summary: Interpretation: deciding what the song means and letting that change how you sing it.
objectives: You will say what your song is about and who you are singing to
You will mark two moments to change
You will sing it with those choices
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Write one sentence: what happens in this song
- Mark one place to get quieter and one to open up
- Sing it with your choices, not just the notes

## Understand it

Technique gets the notes right; **interpretation** makes people feel something. Great singers are storytellers.

**Start with the story.** Write **one sentence**: what happens in this song? Who is singing, to whom, and why? ("Someone begging a friend to forgive them before they leave.") Every choice should serve that.

**Plan the shape:**

- **Dynamics** — where should it be **quieter** (intimate, a confession, a memory)? Where should it **open up** (the emotional peak, often the last chorus)? Mark one place for each at first.
- **Build** — most songs grow: verses calmer, choruses bigger, the final chorus biggest. Do not use everything in the first verse.
- **Colour** — breathy for tender lines, brighter for joy, darker for sadness.
- **Rhythm and phrasing** — a slight delay on an important word, a held note, a word spoken rather than sung.

**Make it yours, but truthfully.** Copying a famous singer's every run sounds like an impression. Use what you love about their performance, but sing it as **you** mean it.

**Runs and riffs** (fast decorative notes — common in gospel, R&B and Afrobeats) should serve the emotion, not decorate every line. Master the plain melody first.

Test your choices: record two versions with different interpretations and ask which tells the story better.

## Key words

- **Interpretation:** the singer's choices about how to express a song
- **Build:** growing in intensity through a song
- **Run (riff):** a quick decorative series of notes

lessons.title: Stage presence and nerves
lessons.summary: What to do with your body and your fear in front of people.
objectives: You will stand and move with purpose
You will use a breathing routine to settle nerves
You will make eye contact with an audience
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Walk on, stand still, breathe, then begin
- Practise the slow breath that settles the heart rate
- Sing to three points in the room, not the floor

## Understand it

Nerves are normal — even for professionals. **Stage fright** is the body's alarm response (adrenaline): fast heartbeat, shallow breathing, dry mouth, shaking. The aim is not to feel nothing, but to **manage it** so it becomes energy rather than panic.

**Calming the body:**

- **Slow breathing** — breathe in for 4 counts, out for 6–8. A longer out-breath activates the body's calming system and slows the heart. Do this before you walk on.
- **Shake out** tension — hands, shoulders, jaw.
- **Sip water** for a dry mouth.

**Preparation is the best cure:**

- Know the song so well that it **runs automatically**, even when nervous.
- Practise **performing** — to family, friends, a phone camera — not only practising.
- **Visualise** the performance going well, in detail.

**Stage presence:**

- **Walk on with purpose**, stand still, find your position.
- **Breathe, then begin** — never rush the start. A moment of stillness looks confident.
- **Look at the audience** — or just above their heads if eye contact is too much.
- **Stillness** — avoid swaying, fidgeting or gripping the mic stand. Gestures should come from the song.
- **If you make a mistake**, keep going and keep your face calm; most of the audience will not notice.
- **Finish fully** — hold the end, then acknowledge the applause (a smile, a nod, "thank you").

## Key words

- **Adrenaline:** the hormone behind stage nerves
- **Stage presence:** the confidence and focus that hold an audience
- **Visualisation:** rehearsing a performance in your mind

## What to do

- Warm up properly, then perform your song
- Use your interpretation choices and your mic technique
- Give two classmates one useful note each

## Understand it

The showcase is where every part of the course meets: posture, breath, resonance, diction, range, mic technique, interpretation and stage presence.

**Before the day:**

- **Know the song completely** — words, melody, the backing track or accompaniment, the start and end.
- **Rehearse with the mic** and backing you will actually use.
- **Plan your interpretation** — the story, where it gets quieter, where it opens up.
- **Rest your voice** the day before — no shouting, plenty of water and sleep.

**On the day:**

1. **Warm up properly** (10–15 minutes): body, breath, lip trills, sirens, scales — gentle to demanding.
2. **Sound check**: sing your loudest and softest parts.
3. **Breathe slowly** before you go on.

**During:** walk on, settle, breathe, begin. Tell the story. Use the mic. Hold the ending.

**After — reflection:**

- Listen to a recording if you can.
- **What went well?** Be specific ("my high note in the chorus was supported and in tune").
- **What to work on next?** One or two specific goals ("breathing before the second verse", "diction on fast lines").
- **Feedback from others**, given and received respectfully.

Then, rest your voice. A performance is demanding; give the folds a quiet evening.

## Key words

- **Showcase:** a performance that shows what has been learnt
- **Reflection:** reviewing a performance to set new goals
- **Vocal rest:** a period of quiet to let the voice recover

lessons.title: What a studio is now
lessons.summary: A DAW on a phone or a laptop, and the four jobs every record goes through.
objectives: You will open a project in a free DAW
You will name the four stages: write, record, mix, master
You will save and find your project again
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Install BandLab (phone or browser) or Cakewalk (Windows) — both free
- Make a project, name it properly, save it
- Play with the transport: play, stop, loop

## Understand it

Not long ago, recording music needed an expensive studio full of hardware. Today, a **DAW** (Digital Audio Workstation) on a laptop or phone does the work of the whole studio: recording, editing, instruments, effects and mixing. Many hit records — including Nigerian Afrobeats hits — began on a laptop in a bedroom.

**Free DAWs to start with:**

- **BandLab** — runs in a browser or phone app; easy, with built-in instruments and loops, and online collaboration.
- **Cakewalk** (Windows) — a full professional DAW, free from BandLab.
- **GarageBand** (Apple devices).

Others (FL Studio, Ableton Live, Logic Pro) are paid, but the skills transfer — every DAW shares the same core ideas.

**What every DAW has:**

- **Tracks** — one per instrument or sound, stacked vertically.
- **The timeline** — time flows left to right, divided into bars and beats.
- **Audio tracks** (recorded sound) and **MIDI tracks** (note information that plays virtual instruments).
- **The mixer** — volume, panning and effects for each track.
- **Transport** — play, stop, record, loop.

**Good habits from day one:**

lessons.title: Tempo, the grid, and your first beat
lessons.summary: How a DAW counts time, and placing sounds on the grid.
objectives: You will set a tempo in bpm
You will place kick and snare on the grid
You will loop four bars
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Set the tempo to 100 bpm
- Place a kick on beats 1 and 3, a snare on 2 and 4
- Loop the bar and listen

## Understand it

Everything in a DAW sits on the **grid** — bars and beats laid out on the timeline, set by the **tempo**.

**Tempo (bpm)** decides the speed and often the genre:

- **Hip-hop**: around 80–100 bpm.
- **Afrobeats / amapiano**: often 100–115 bpm.
- **House**: around 120–128 bpm.
- **Drum and bass**: around 170 bpm.

Set the tempo **before** you start; changing it later affects recorded audio.

**Your first beat** — the backbeat that underpins most popular music:

- Set **4/4** time at **100 bpm**.
- **Kick** on beats **1 and 3**.
- **Snare** (or clap) on beats **2 and 4**.
- **Loop** the bar so it repeats.

You can program this in the **piano roll** or **step sequencer** — a grid where each square is a step (often 16 to a bar: sixteenth notes). Click a square to place a hit.

**Quantise** — snapping notes exactly onto the grid. Useful to tidy timing, but 100% quantised beats can sound robotic; producers often keep a little looseness or add **swing** (delaying every second sixteenth slightly) for groove.

**The metronome / click** helps you play in and record in time.

The grid is your map: learn to count in bars (1, 2, 3, 4 — 2, 2, 3, 4 …) so you always know where you are in the song.

## Key words

- **Grid:** the bars and beats on the DAW timeline
- **BPM:** beats per minute — the tempo
- **Step sequencer:** a grid for placing drum hits
- **Quantise:** snapping notes to the grid

lessons.title: Drum programming
lessons.summary: Hi-hats, swing, velocity, and making a programmed beat sound played.
objectives: You will add hi-hats and a second percussion layer
You will change velocity so notes are not all identical
You will nudge a note off the grid on purpose
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Add eighth-note hi-hats, then vary their velocity
- Add one Nigerian percussion sound — shaker, conga, agogo
- Nudge one hit slightly late and hear it loosen

## Understand it

A basic kick-and-snare beat becomes a real groove with **hi-hats**, **velocity** and **percussion**.

**Hi-hats** fill the space between kick and snare:

- **Eighth notes** (8 per bar) — a steady pulse.
- **Sixteenth notes** (16 per bar) — busier, more energy.
- **Rolls and triplets** — trap and Afrobeats use fast hi-hat rolls at the ends of phrases.
- **Open hi-hat** on some off-beats adds lift.

**Velocity** — how hard each note is hit (in MIDI, 1–127). A real drummer never hits two strokes identically. If every hi-hat is the same velocity, the beat sounds **robotic**. Vary them: accents louder on the beat, softer between, slight random variation. This is often the single biggest improvement in a beginner's beat.

**Nigerian percussion** gives a beat its identity. Add one:

- **Shekere** — a gourd covered with a net of beads; a shaking, rattling sound.
- **Talking drum (dùndún)** — pitch-bending drum.
- **Agogo** — a double bell.
- **Log drum** — the deep, melodic bass hits central to amapiano.
- **Congas** and **djembe** patterns.

They often play **syncopated** patterns — accents between the main beats — which create the rolling, danceable feel of Afrobeats.

Use percussion samples from your DAW's library, or record your own (always clearly and with permission).

## Key words

- **Velocity:** how hard a MIDI note is played (1–127)
- **Syncopation:** accents falling between the main beats
- **Shekere:** a West African gourd rattle covered in beads
- **Sample:** a short recorded sound used in a track

lessons.title: Chords and melody
lessons.summary: Adding a virtual instrument, and writing something over the beat.
objectives: You will add a software instrument
You will play or draw a four-chord progression
You will write a melody over it
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Add a piano or synth track
- Draw a four-chord loop — try Am F C G
- Write a short melody using notes from those chords

## Understand it

Chords give a track its **emotion** and **harmony**; the melody gives it something to sing.

**Chords** are three or more notes played together. **Major chords** sound bright or happy; **minor chords** sound darker or sad. A **chord progression** is a repeating sequence of chords.

**Am – F – C – G** is one of the most used progressions in popular music (it is the same four chords as C – G – Am – F, starting in a different place). In the piano roll:

- **Am** = A, C, E
- **F** = F, A, C
- **C** = C, E, G
- **G** = G, B, D

Give each chord **one bar**, and loop the four bars.

**Writing a melody over it:**

- Use notes from the **scale** the chords come from — here, the **C major / A minor** scale (all white keys on a keyboard). They will all fit.
- **Chord tones** (notes in the current chord) on strong beats sound stable; other notes passing between them add movement.
- Keep it **simple and singable** — a short idea, repeated with small changes. Most memorable melodies use few notes.
- **Rhythm** matters as much as pitch: repetition of a rhythm makes a hook.
- Leave **space** — gaps make a melody breathe and leave room for vocals.

Try playing ideas on a MIDI keyboard or your computer keyboard, record them, and keep the best.

## Key words

- **Chord:** three or more notes played together
- **Chord progression:** a repeating sequence of chords
- **Chord tone:** a melody note that belongs to the current chord
- **Hook:** the catchiest, most memorable part of a song

lessons.title: Recording a voice
lessons.summary: Mic, gain, room, and getting a clean take with what you actually have.
objectives: You will set a recording level that does not clip
You will reduce room noise with what you have
You will record and keep the best take
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Set gain so the loudest part peaks around -6 dB, never at 0
- Record in a small soft space — a wardrobe beats a big room
- Record three takes, keep the best, label it

## Understand it

A great vocal recording starts **before** you press record. Most problems cannot be fixed later.

**Gain staging** — setting the input level:

- Ask the singer to perform their **loudest** part while you adjust the input **gain**.
- Aim for peaks around **−12 to −6 dBFS** on the meter — comfortably below 0.
- **0 dBFS is the ceiling.** Any signal hitting it **clips** — harsh, crunchy digital distortion that **cannot be removed** afterwards.
- Too low is better than too high: quiet recordings can be turned up; clipped ones are ruined.

**The room matters more than the microphone:**

- Hard, bare walls cause **reflections** — echo and boxiness.
- Record in a **small, soft space**: a wardrobe full of clothes, a room with curtains, mattresses or blankets around the singer. Many home producers record in a closet.
- Avoid noise: fans, generators, traffic, phones. Turn off the AC while recording.

**Mic technique:**

- About **15–20 cm** from the mouth.
- A **pop filter** (or a sock over a wire hanger) stops plosive pops on "p" and "b".
- Singer stays at a consistent distance.

**Headphones** for the singer — closed-back, so the backing track does not leak into the mic.

**Record several takes**; later you can choose the best parts (**comping**).

## Key words

- **Gain:** the input level of a recording
- **Clipping:** distortion when a signal exceeds 0 dBFS
- **Pop filter:** a screen that stops plosive bursts
- **Comping:** combining the best parts of several takes

## Read and watch

lessons.title: Arrangement
lessons.summary: Turning a loop into a song: intro, verse, chorus, and a reason to keep listening.
objectives: You will build a song structure from your loop
You will add and remove parts between sections
You will say why a chorus should feel bigger
lessons.body:
## What to do

- Map out intro, verse, chorus, verse, chorus, outro
- Take parts AWAY in the verse so the chorus feels bigger by contrast
- Add one new sound at the chorus

## Understand it

**Arrangement** is how a song is organised over time — which sections come when, and which instruments play in each. A loop that plays unchanged for three minutes is boring; arrangement creates a journey.

**A common song structure:**

**Intro → Verse → Chorus → Verse → Chorus → Bridge → Chorus → Outro**

- **Intro** — sets the mood; often a few elements.
- **Verse** — tells the story; usually calmer.
- **Pre-chorus** (optional) — builds tension.
- **Chorus** — the hook, the biggest and most memorable section.
- **Bridge** — something different, for contrast before the final chorus.
- **Outro** — the ending.

Afrobeats and amapiano often use longer instrumental sections, call-and-response, and dropping elements in and out over a steady groove.

**The key idea: contrast through subtraction.** Producers make choruses feel big mainly by taking parts **away** in the verses — fewer drums, no bass in the first verse, filtered sounds — so that when everything comes in at the chorus, it **hits**.

**Other tools:**

- **Build-ups** — rising sounds, snare rolls, filters opening.
- **Drops and breaks** — a moment of silence or only one element before the chorus.
- **Variation** — change something every 4–8 bars so the ear stays interested.

Map the arrangement first: draw the sections as blocks on the timeline and decide what plays in each.

## Key words

- **Arrangement:** the organisation of sections and instruments over time
- **Verse / chorus:** storytelling sections / the repeated hook section
- **Bridge:** a contrasting section before the final chorus
- **Build-up:** rising tension leading into a big section

## Read and watch

## What to do

- Open the week 2 beat and listen to it honestly
- Rebuild it from scratch with velocity, layers and arrangement

## Understand it

Producers often say their skills improve faster than their taste lets them notice. Rebuilding your week 2 beat **from scratch**, with five weeks' more knowledge, shows exactly how far you have come.

**First, listen honestly** to the week 2 beat. Write down what is weak — common answers: robotic hi-hats, drums that do not hit, nothing changes, no identity.

**Rebuild with what you now know:**

- **Velocity** variation on hi-hats and percussion (week 3).
- **Layering** — combine two sounds for one part: a punchy kick with a sub kick under it; a snare layered with a clap. Make sure layers **line up exactly** in time.
- **Percussion** with identity — shekere, talking drum, log drum, congas.
- **Syncopation** — some hits between the beats.
- **Swing** — a little delay on off-beat sixteenths for groove.
- **Variation** — a change every 4 or 8 bars (a fill, a dropout, a new percussion part).
- **Space** — not every step filled. Silence makes the hits hit.

**Compare**: export both versions and play them **side by side** at the **same volume** (louder always sounds "better", so match levels for a fair test). Ask someone else which they prefer, and why.

Keep notes on what made the biggest difference — that is your personal production knowledge.

- **Layering:** combining sounds to make one fuller sound
- **Swing:** delaying off-beat notes for a groovier feel

lessons.title: Mixing I: level and space
lessons.summary: Balance and panning — the two moves that fix most amateur mixes.
objectives: You will balance levels so nothing buries anything
You will pan parts across the stereo field

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Pull every fader down and rebuild the balance from the kick up
- Pan: keep kick, bass and lead vocal centre; move others out
- Mix quietly — loud mixing hides problems

## Understand it

**Mixing** is the art of balancing all the tracks so every part is heard clearly and the whole sounds good on any speaker. The first two tools are the simplest and the most important: **level** (volume) and **pan** (left–right position).

**Level — build the balance from the bottom up:**

1. Pull **every fader down**.
2. Bring up the **kick** to a healthy level (peaking around −10 dB on the master).
3. Add the **bass** — balance it with the kick so both are clear.
4. Add **snare/clap**, then other drums.
5. Add the **lead vocal** — usually the most important element; it must sit clearly on top.
6. Add everything else around them.

Leave **headroom** — the master should not go near 0 dB. A mix peaking around −6 dB is fine.

**Pan — use the stereo space:**

- **Centre**: kick, snare, bass and lead vocal — the foundation and focus.
- **Sides**: hi-hats slightly off-centre, percussion, guitars, keys, backing vocals spread left and right.
- Balance — if something is panned left, put something similar on the right.

**Check your mix:**

- At **low volume** — the balance shows more clearly.
- On **different speakers** — headphones, phone speaker, car. Most listeners hear music on phones.
- **In mono** — everything should still be heard.

Take breaks: ears tire quickly, and a tired ear makes bad decisions.

## Key words

- **Mixing:** balancing tracks into a finished whole
- **Fader:** the volume control for a track
- **Pan:** a sound's left–right position
- **Headroom:** space below 0 dB on the master

lessons.title: Mixing II: EQ and compression
lessons.summary: Cutting what is in the way, and evening out what jumps around.
objectives: You will cut a frequency range rather than boosting everything
You will apply gentle compression to a vocal
You will say what a compressor actually does
lessons.body:
## What to do

- High-pass everything that is not bass or kick
- Cut, do not boost, where two parts fight
- Compress the vocal gently: a few dB of reduction, no more

## Understand it

**EQ** (equalisation) and **compression** are the two most-used mixing tools.

**EQ** adjusts the balance of **frequencies** in a sound — bass, mids and treble. Every sound occupies part of the **frequency spectrum** (from about 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz):

- **Low end (20–250 Hz)** — kick, bass, the weight.
- **Mids (250 Hz–4 kHz)** — most instruments and the voice's body.
- **Highs (4–20 kHz)** — clarity, air, cymbals, sibilance.

Rules of thumb:

- **High-pass filter** (cut the lows) on everything that is not bass or kick — vocals, guitars, keys, hi-hats have useless low rumble that muddies the mix.
- **Cut before you boost.** When two parts fight (e.g. kick and bass, vocal and keys), cut a little of the clashing frequency in one, rather than boosting the other.
- Small moves (2–4 dB) usually beat big ones.

**Compression** reduces the **dynamic range** — the difference between loud and soft — by turning down the loudest moments. It makes a vocal sit steadily in the mix and drums sound punchier.

The controls:

- **Threshold** — the level above which compression starts.
- **Ratio** — how strongly it turns down (4:1 is common for vocals).
- **Attack/release** — how fast it reacts and recovers.
- **Gain reduction meter** — aim for about **3–6 dB** on peaks for a vocal.

Too much compression sounds squashed and lifeless. **Bypass** often to compare.

## Key words

- **EQ:** adjusting the balance of frequencies
- **High-pass filter:** cuts low frequencies below a set point
- **Compression:** reducing the difference between loud and soft
- **Threshold / ratio:** where compression starts / how strongly it acts

1. Mix one song using cuts only, no boosts
1. Bypass each plugin and ask honestly whether it helped

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Run a stem splitter on a song and listen for the artefacts it leaves
- Run your week 9 mix through a free AI mastering service, then compare with your own
- Read who owns AI-generated audio, and what you must declare

## Understand it

AI tools now do real jobs in music production. Knowing what each does well — and where it goes wrong — makes you a better producer rather than a replaced one.

**What these tools do:**

- **Stem separation** — splitting a finished song into vocals, drums, bass and other parts. Useful for remixes, practice and sampling — but listen for **artefacts**: watery, swirling or metallic sounds, cymbals bleeding into the vocal, missing transients.
- **Automatic mixing and mastering** — services that analyse a track and apply EQ, compression and loudness. Fast and often decent, but they apply **generic** decisions: they do not know which element you want to lead, or the style you intend. Compare against your own mix at matched loudness.
- **Generated music** — whole tracks from a text prompt. Results can sound polished but generic, and they raise serious questions.

**Questions every producer should ask:**

- **Rights** — who owns generated or separated material? Samples from someone else's song still need **permission (clearance)**, even if a tool extracted them. Distributors and platforms increasingly require you to declare generated content.
- **Training data** — many models were trained on artists' work without consent or payment; musicians and organisations are challenging this.
- **Your voice** — tools that clone a singer's voice must never be used on a real person without their permission.

**The skill:** use tools for **tasks** (cleaning audio, separating stems for practice, a reference master), and keep the **creative decisions** — what the song says, how it feels — yours. Always **trust your ears over the tool**.

## Key words

- **Stem separation:** splitting a mixed song into separate parts
- **Artefact:** an unwanted sound left by processing
- **Clearance:** permission to use someone else's recording
- **Mastering:** the final processing of a mixed track for release

## Read and watch

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Export a WAV for distribution and an MP3 for sharing
- Fill in the metadata: title, artist, year, credits
- Credit every musician and writer by name

## Understand it

A finished track must be exported correctly and labelled properly before the world can hear it — and get you paid.

**Exporting (bouncing):**

- **WAV** (uncompressed, e.g. 24-bit or 16-bit, 44.1 kHz) — full quality. Use it for **distribution**, mastering and archiving.
- **MP3** (compressed, e.g. 320 kbps) — much smaller, slight loss of quality. Use it for **sharing** on WhatsApp, email, demos.
- Check the export **does not clip** and that the start and end are clean (no cut-off reverb tails).

**Loudness:** streaming platforms adjust tracks to a similar loudness, so making a master as loud as possible does not make it sound louder there — it just makes it more distorted. Aim for a clean, dynamic master.

**Metadata** — the information attached to the track:

- Title, **artist name** (spelt exactly the same every time), year, genre.
- **Songwriters and producers** — credits matter for royalties.
- **Cover art** — usually 3000 × 3000 pixels, square, with no blurry text.
- **ISRC** — an international code that identifies each recording; distributors usually provide it.
- **Explicit** or clean.

**Distribution** — to get on Spotify, Apple Music, Audiomack, Boomplay and YouTube Music, you go through a **distributor** (many exist, some free). Read their terms carefully: what percentage they take, whether you keep ownership.

**Rights:** you must own or have permission for everything in the track — beats, samples, vocals.

## Key words

- **WAV:** an uncompressed full-quality audio file
- **MP3:** a compressed, smaller audio file
- **Metadata:** information attached to a track, like title and credits
- **ISRC:** the international code identifying a recording

## Read and watch

lessons.body:
## What to do

- Play your finished track to the class
- Explain three decisions: arrangement, mix, and one creative choice
- Take notes from two classmates and apply one

## Understand it

Releasing a track — even only to the class — finishes the creative cycle: **make, finish, share, learn**. Most beginners never finish; finishing is a skill.

**Presenting your track:**

- Play it on decent speakers at a **moderate volume**.
- Explain **three decisions** you made:
  1. **Arrangement** — how the song is structured, and how you created contrast (what drops out, what builds).
  2. **Mix** — one specific choice ("I high-passed the keys so the bass is clearer", "I panned the shekere left and the hi-hat right").
  3. **One creative risk** — something you tried that you were not sure about.

**Giving and receiving feedback:**

- Be **specific**: "the kick and bass clash in the chorus" helps; "it's nice" does not.
- Start with what works, then one suggestion.
- When receiving feedback, **listen and note it**, without defending. You do not have to agree — but if several people say the same thing, it is probably true.

**Reflect on the term:**

- What can you do now that you could not in week 1?
- What is your **next skill** to learn — sound design, recording, mixing, songwriting?
- What will your **next track** be?

**Protect your work**: back up the project and the final WAV in two places. Keep stems — you may want to remix it later.

And look after your hearing — it is the only tool you cannot replace.

## Key words

- **Release:** making a finished track available to listeners
- **Stems:** separate exported groups of tracks (drums, bass, vocals)
- **Constructive feedback:** specific, useful comments that help improve work
